cards.title: Why can the baseline-predictor slope stay unchanged across equivalent group codings?
cards.answer: The group-mean space is unchanged, so adjusting for it leaves the same regression problem for the numeric predictor, assuming identifiability.
cards.takeaway: Recoding a nuisance factor does not add or remove adjustment directions.

sources.locator: HW2 · Q1 and Q4 · companion concept check

cards.title: What is the Gaussian maximum-likelihood estimate of \(\sigma ^{2}\) when \(\operatorname{SSE}>0\)?
cards.answer: \(\operatorname{SSE}/n\), rather than \(\operatorname{SSE}/(n-r)\).
cards.takeaway: Maximum likelihood and unbiasedness optimize different criteria.

sources.locator: HW2 · Q7; least-squares theory · companion concept check
Least-squares theory · variance estimator · companion concept check

cards.title: Why is \(\operatorname{SSE}/n\) downward biased under the correct mean model?
cards.answer: Fitting removes noise along r model directions, leaving expected \(\operatorname{SSE}=(n-r)\sigma ^{2}\).
cards.takeaway: The residual has already had some noise fitted away.

sources.locator: HW2 · Q7; least-squares theory · companion concept check
Least-squares theory · variance estimator · companion concept check

cards.title: If \(\operatorname{rank}(X)=n\), can \(\operatorname{SSE}/(n-\operatorname{rank}(X))\) estimate noise variance?
cards.answer: No. There are no residual degrees of freedom, and the denominator is zero.
cards.takeaway: A saturated fit leaves no independent residual noise to measure.

sources.locator: HW2 · Q7; least-squares theory · companion concept check
Least-squares theory · variance estimator · companion concept check
HW2 · Q7; least-squares theory · companion concept check
Least-squares theory · variance estimator · companion concept check

cards.title: If Gaussian \(\operatorname{SSE}=0\), is \(\hat{\sigma}^{2}=0\) an ordinary positive interior MLE?
cards.answer: No. The likelihood grows as variance approaches zero, a boundary behavior.
cards.takeaway: A formula at the boundary needs separate interpretation.
cards.source: HW2 · Q7; least-squares theory · companion practice

cards.title: Does Gauss–Markov require normal errors?
cards.answer: No. The mean and equal-variance, uncorrelated-error assumptions are enough for the linear-unbiased comparison.
cards.takeaway: Normality is not part of BLUE’s core argument.

cards.title: Can a slightly biased estimator outperform the best linear unbiased estimator in squared error?
cards.answer: Yes. A reduction in variance can outweigh the squared bias. “Best linear unbiased” (BLUE) only compares variance among linear estimators with zero bias.
cards.takeaway: Accepting some bias can reduce variance enough to help overall error.

cards.title: Does \(\operatorname{Var}(y)=\sigma ^{2}I\) mean the errors are independent?
cards.answer: It says they have equal variances and zero pairwise covariances. Independence follows if they are jointly Gaussian, but not from this covariance statement alone.
cards.takeaway: A covariance model is weaker than a full distribution model.

cards.title: When does the generalized-inverse condition force \(G=B^{-1}\)?
cards.answer: When B is invertible. Multiply \(BGB=B\) by \(B^{-1}\) on both sides.
cards.takeaway: Full invertibility removes the freedom.

sources.locator: Linear algebra notes · pp. 4–5 · companion concept check
Linear algebra notes · pp. 4–5 · companion concept check

cards.title: Which \(\operatorname{diag}(1,t)\) is the Moore–Penrose inverse of \(\operatorname{diag}(1,0)\)?
cards.takeaway: The pseudoinverse avoids arbitrary action in the null direction.
cards.source: Linear algebra notes · pp. 4–5 · companion practice

cards.title: How does the fitted-value projector act on C(X) and \(C(X)^{\perp}\)?
cards.answer: It keeps the first and kills the second.
cards.takeaway: Those two actions completely determine the projection.

cards.title: If an alternative fit differs from the projection by length 3, how much extra squared error does it add?
cards.answer: 9, by the orthogonal squared-distance decomposition.
cards.takeaway: Distance within the model adds in quadrature.

cards.title: For full-rank X, when is By unbiased for \(\beta\) for every \(\beta\)?
cards.answer: When \(BX=I\), because \(E[By]=BX\beta\).
cards.takeaway: Unbiasedness becomes a matrix identity.

sources.locator: Least-squares theory · pp. 19–20 · companion concept check

cards.title: Why is \(AA^{\mathsf{T}}\) positive semidefinite?
cards.answer: For every v, \(v^{\mathsf{T}}AA^{\mathsf{T}}v=\Vert A^{\mathsf{T}}v\Vert ^{2}\ge 0\).
cards.takeaway: A squared length can never reduce variance.

sources.locator: Least-squares theory · pp. 19–20 · companion concept check

cards.title: Are GLS residuals necessarily Euclidean-orthogonal to X’s columns?
cards.answer: No. They satisfy \(X^{\mathsf{T}}V^{-1}e=0\): weighted orthogonality.
cards.takeaway: GLS changes the geometry used to measure angles and lengths.

sources.locator: Least-squares theory · pp. 20–22 · companion concept check
Least-squares theory · pp. 20–22 · companion concept check

cards.title: If \(\operatorname{Var}(y)=\sigma ^{2}V\), what covariance does \(V^{-\frac{1}{2}}y\) have?
cards.takeaway: Whitening removes unequal scales and covariance in the transformed coordinates.

cards.title: An average combines m independent equal-variance observations. What precision weight should it get?
cards.answer: Weight proportional to m, since its variance is \(\sigma ^{2}/m\).
cards.takeaway: More independent measurements make an average more precise.

sources.locator: Least-squares theory · p. 22 · companion concept check

cards.title: Are inverse marginal variances alone enough for GLS with correlated errors?
cards.answer: No. The full inverse covariance matters, including off-diagonal entries.
cards.takeaway: Correlation changes which combinations are informative.

sources.locator: Least-squares theory · p. 22 · companion concept check

cards.title: Under the Gaussian linear model, what is \(\operatorname{SSE}/\sigma ^{2}\) distributed as?
cards.answer: \(\chi ^{2}\) with \(n-\operatorname{rank}(X)\) degrees of freedom, assuming positive residual df.
cards.takeaway: Residual noise lives in the unfitted directions.

sources.locator: Inference notes · p. 3 · companion concept check

cards.title: Does a projector always turn squared noise length into a chi-squared variable?
cards.answer: No. The exact chi-squared result requires the appropriate Gaussian noise model.
cards.takeaway: Geometry alone does not determine the noise distribution.

sources.locator: Inference notes · p. 3 · companion concept check
Inference notes · p. 3 · companion concept check

cards.title: Why is \(H(I-H)=0\)?
cards.answer: \(H-H^{2}=0\) because H is idempotent.
cards.takeaway: The fitted and residual projectors keep disjoint directions.

cards.title: Why use the full model’s residual SSE in the F-test denominator?
cards.answer: It estimates noise after allowing all directions under consideration.
cards.takeaway: Use the leftover variation as the noise benchmark.

sources.locator: Inference notes · pp. 3–6 · companion concept check

cards.title: Under the null, why is an F statistic often near 1 rather than 0?
cards.answer: Both numerator and denominator estimate the same noise variance after dividing by their degrees of freedom.
cards.takeaway: Added directions fit some noise even when no effect exists.

sources.locator: Inference notes · pp. 3–6 · companion concept check

cards.title: For \(F=5\) with 2 added directions and 20 residual df, what reference is needed for a p-value?
cards.answer: F with degrees of freedom (2,20), under the Gaussian null assumptions.
cards.takeaway: A statistic’s value is not itself its tail probability.

sources.locator: Inference notes · p. 5 · companion calculation · companion concept check
Inference notes · pp. 5–6 · companion concept check

cards.title: For positive SSEs in nested Gaussian models, what is the null/full maximized likelihood ratio?
cards.answer: \((\operatorname{SSE}_{0}/\operatorname{SSE}_{1})^{-n/2}\). Larger relative improvement makes this ratio smaller.
cards.takeaway: The simpler model loses likelihood when its residual cost rises.

cards.title: Why can’t every coefficient restriction be tested in a rank-deficient model?
cards.answer: Some restrictions change along null directions while the data distribution stays the same.
cards.takeaway: A hypothesis must concern observable information.

sources.locator: Inference notes · pp. 8–10 · companion concept check
Inference notes · pp. 8–10 · companion concept check

cards.title: How do you encode \(\beta _{1}=\beta _{2}\) and \(\beta _{3}=2\) for \(\beta =(\beta _{0},\beta _{1},\beta _{2},\beta _{3})\)?
cards.answer: Use rows (0,1,−1,0) and (0,0,0,1), with targets 0 and 2.
cards.takeaway: Each independent row represents one constraint.

sources.locator: Inference notes · pp. 8–10 · companion concept check

cards.title: In the constrained least-squares block system, what does the lower block enforce?
cards.answer: \(\Lambda \beta =c\).
cards.takeaway: One block optimizes; the other keeps the solution feasible.

sources.locator: Inference notes · pp. 8–10 · companion concept check

cards.title: What is the stationarity equation for constrained least squares?
cards.answer: \(X^{\mathsf{T}}X\beta +\Lambda ^{\mathsf{T}}\xi =X^{\mathsf{T}}y\), with multiplier scaling absorbed in \(\xi\).
cards.takeaway: The constraint supplies the force balancing the loss gradient.

cards.title: Why use a t distribution instead of a standard normal when \(\sigma\) is estimated?
cards.answer: The estimated noise scale introduces extra uncertainty. Under Gaussian errors, the standardized coefficient uses t with n−p df.
cards.takeaway: Estimating the denominator makes the tails heavier.

sources.locator: Inference notes · p. 10 · companion concept check
Inference notes · p. 10 · companion concept check

cards.title: A coefficient is 1.2 with SE 0.6. What t statistic tests zero?
cards.takeaway: A t statistic measures distance from the null in SE units.

cards.title: How do you build a pointwise coefficient confidence interval?
cards.answer: Estimate \(\pm\) t critical value \(\times\) estimated SE, under the Gaussian linear-model conditions.
cards.takeaway: Uncertainty is a margin around the estimate.

sources.locator: Inference notes · p. 10 · companion concept check
Inference notes · p. 10 · companion concept check

cards.title: Does a frequentist 95% interval assign 95% posterior probability to its parameter range?
cards.answer: No. That interpretation needs a posterior distribution and its assumptions.
cards.takeaway: Coverage and posterior probability are different statements.

cards.title: Can unlimited data eliminate uncertainty in a new noisy response?
cards.answer: It can eliminate mean-estimation uncertainty in suitable settings, but not the new response’s irreducible noise.
cards.takeaway: Learning the average perfectly does not predict every outcome perfectly.

sources.locator: Inference notes · pp. 12–13 · companion concept check

cards.title: If ten independent intervals each cover with probability 0.95, what is their joint coverage?
cards.takeaway: Many individually reliable statements can be jointly unreliable.

sources.locator: Inference notes · pp. 11–12 · companion concept check

cards.title: If \(E[Y]=\mu\), what is \(E[AY+b]\)?
cards.takeaway: Expectation follows affine transformations directly.

sources.locator: Inference notes · p. 1 · companion concept check

cards.title: Does \(\operatorname{Var}(AY)=A\Sigma A^{\mathsf{T}}\) require Gaussian Y?
cards.answer: No. Finite second moments suffice.
cards.takeaway: Moment identities are more general than Gaussian distribution results.

sources.locator: Inference notes · p. 1 · companion concept check
Inference notes · p. 1 · companion concept check

cards.title: When does zero covariance imply independence for two random vectors?
cards.answer: When they are jointly Gaussian.
cards.takeaway: Separate Gaussian marginals alone are not enough.

cards.title: Can \(x_{3}\approx x_{1}+x_{2}\) cause multicollinearity without an almost-perfect pairwise correlation?
cards.answer: Yes. The near-dependence uses three columns together.
cards.takeaway: Look for weak directions in the entire design.

sources.locator: Inference notes · pp. 14–15 · companion concept check
Inference notes · pp. 14–15 · companion concept check

cards.title: Why can stable training predictions become unstable off the observed predictor relationship?
cards.answer: The cancellation between uncertain coefficients may no longer occur at the new predictor values.
cards.takeaway: A weakly identified direction can become visible during extrapolation.

cards.title: If a predictor has \(R^{2}=0\) against the others, what is its VIF?
cards.answer: 1. There is no variance inflation from linear overlap under this comparison.
cards.takeaway: No overlap means no inflation beyond the baseline.

sources.locator: Inference notes · pp. 15–18 · companion concept check

cards.title: Does a large VIF automatically mean you should delete a predictor?
cards.answer: No. The scientific target and model assumptions matter too.
cards.takeaway: A warning about uncertainty is not a complete modeling decision.

sources.locator: Inference notes · pp. 15–18 · companion concept check

cards.title: What does a zero Gram–Schmidt residual mean?
cards.answer: The new column is already in the earlier span.
cards.takeaway: The column adds no independent information.

sources.locator: Inference notes · pp. 20–23 · companion concept check

cards.title: How do you turn a nonzero orthogonal residual u into a unit vector?
cards.answer: Divide by \(\Vert u\Vert\).
cards.takeaway: Orthogonal means perpendicular; orthonormal also means unit length.

sources.locator: Inference notes · pp. 20–23 · companion concept check

cards.title: Why might discarding small principal components help even though it loses information?
cards.answer: It can reduce variance by removing poorly determined directions, at the cost of bias.
cards.takeaway: A smaller model trades flexibility for stability.

sources.locator: Inference notes · pp. 23–24 · companion concept check

cards.title: Does using y to build PLS components guarantee better predictions than PCR?
cards.answer: No. Response-informed directions can also fit noise. Compare honest held-out performance.
cards.takeaway: Supervision is useful information, not a performance guarantee.

sources.locator: Inference notes · pp. 24–25 · companion concept check

cards.title: What connects a data question to a useful decision?
cards.answer: Collect and clean relevant data, explore patterns, fit and evaluate models, then communicate an actionable result.
cards.takeaway: The model is one step in the project.

cards.title: Why define the prediction question before choosing features?
cards.answer: It determines the target, prediction time, and information actually available when making the decision.
cards.takeaway: A useful prediction must be possible at the moment it is needed.

cards.title: Why can .isna() miss missing observations?
cards.answer: It checks cells in existing rows. An entirely absent row has no cells to inspect.
cards.takeaway: Compare observed records with the records that should exist.

cards.title: How would you find missing hours in an hourly dataset?
cards.answer: Construct the expected timestamp sequence and compare it with observed timestamps.
cards.takeaway: Completeness includes missing records, not just blank values.

cards.title: Why put data cleaning into a repeatable function?
cards.answer: It applies the same transformations consistently and makes decisions inspectable and reproducible.
cards.takeaway: A pipeline records how raw data became analysis data.

cards.title: Why convert normalized temperature back to degrees for interpretation?
cards.answer: A slope per degree is easier to interpret than a slope per arbitrary normalized unit.
cards.takeaway: Units give coefficients practical meaning.

cards.title: Why inspect rider groups separately instead of only their overall average?
cards.answer: A dominant group can hide another group's distinct pattern.
cards.takeaway: An average can conceal different behaviors.

cards.title: Why compare similar hours when studying temperature and rentals?
cards.answer: Time of day affects demand and may differ across temperature ranges, confounding a simple comparison.
cards.takeaway: A pattern can reflect another variable changing alongside the one you study.

cards.title: Why train on an earlier year and evaluate on a later year for forecasting?
cards.answer: It mimics predicting the future using only past information.
cards.takeaway: The evaluation split should resemble deployment.

cards.title: What does negative test \(R^{2}\) reveal?
cards.answer: The predictions have larger squared error than the test-set mean benchmark.
cards.takeaway: A model can fit training data and still fail on new data.

cards.title: What does a curved pattern in residuals suggest?
cards.answer: The model may be missing a nonlinear relationship or another systematic effect.
cards.takeaway: Errors with structure are clues to missing structure in the model.

cards.title: Why can a degree-12 curve fit training data better but predict worse?
cards.answer: Its flexibility can fit accidental noise instead of a stable pattern.
cards.takeaway: Better memorization can mean worse generalization.

cards.title: How can regularization help an overly flexible model?
cards.answer: It discourages large coefficients while still fitting the data.
cards.takeaway: Keep useful flexibility while limiting extreme fits.

cards.title: Why might treating hour as a category beat one numeric hour coefficient?
cards.answer: A single slope imposes a constant hourly change. Categories can represent separate morning and evening peaks.
cards.takeaway: Numeric storage does not require a straight-line effect.

cards.title: How does predicting rental count differ from predicting busy versus quiet?
cards.answer: Count prediction is regression; busy-versus-quiet prediction is classification.
cards.takeaway: The response type determines the task.

cards.title: Why not use an unconstrained straight line as a probability?
cards.answer: It can predict below 0 or above 1. Logistic regression maps a linear score into valid probabilities.
cards.takeaway: A prediction must respect the target's range.

cards.title: How does a decision tree make a prediction?
cards.answer: It follows a sequence of feature-based splits to a terminal prediction.
cards.takeaway: Several simple rules can represent a nonlinear pattern.

cards.title: Why is a 100% success rate from one observation weak evidence?
cards.answer: It has enormous sampling uncertainty; one additional failure changes the estimate dramatically.
cards.takeaway: Extreme percentages can come from tiny samples.

cards.title: How does the estimate \((r+\alpha )/(n+\alpha +\beta )\) stabilize a small-sample proportion?
cards.answer: It combines observed successes and failures with prior pseudo-counts.
cards.takeaway: The prior has more influence when the data are scarce.

cards.title: Why can the most accurate model still be unhelpful operationally?
cards.answer: Its errors or outputs may not match the decision's costs and needs.
cards.takeaway: Evaluate the consequence of being wrong.

cards.title: What three pieces make a recorded value interpretable?
cards.answer: The entity observed, the variable measured, and its value with a meaningful scale.
cards.takeaway: A number without context is ambiguous.

cards.title: How do primary and secondary data differ?
cards.answer: Primary data are collected for the study; secondary data already exist from another collection process.
cards.takeaway: Origin affects what the data can support.

cards.title: How does an API differ from scraping a web page?
cards.answer: An API provides a programmatic data interface; scraping extracts information from page content.
cards.takeaway: Prefer a structured interface when one is available.

cards.title: Why keep API keys out of shared notebooks?
cards.answer: They can grant access or allow requests billed to the owner.
cards.takeaway: A credential is not ordinary example code.

cards.title: What does an API rate limit constrain?
cards.answer: How frequently requests can be made within a specified interval.
cards.takeaway: A working loop can still exceed the service's limits.

cards.title: Does public visibility automatically grant permission to republish data?
cards.answer: No. Visibility and permission to reuse are separate questions; check the applicable license and terms.
cards.takeaway: Accessible does not mean unrestricted.

cards.title: Does robots.txt grant a reuse license?
cards.answer: No. It communicates crawler preferences rather than licensing the content.
cards.takeaway: Different documents answer different permission questions.

cards.title: How can joining two anonymous datasets reveal identities?
cards.answer: Shared attributes can become a distinctive combination that links records to a person.
cards.takeaway: Removing names alone may not remove identifiability.

cards.title: Why cache collected data during analysis?
cards.answer: It avoids repeated downloads, reduces server load, and preserves a reproducible input snapshot.
cards.takeaway: Rerunning analysis should not require refetching unchanged data.

cards.title: What makes a value atomic in a data table?
cards.answer: It is treated as one indivisible value for the analysis, such as a number, Boolean, or label.
cards.takeaway: Atomicity depends on how you use the value.

cards.title: How does a dictionary differ from a single scalar value?
cards.answer: It contains named components that may represent several variables.
cards.takeaway: Nested data often need restructuring before tabular analysis.

cards.title: How do discrete and continuous quantitative variables differ?
cards.answer: Discrete variables have separated possible values; continuous variables can vary throughout an interval in principle.
cards.takeaway: Counts and measurements need different interpretations.

cards.title: What makes a categorical variable nominal?
cards.answer: Its categories have no meaningful intrinsic order, such as blood type.
cards.takeaway: A numeric code does not create an order.

cards.title: What makes a categorical variable ordinal?
cards.answer: Its categories have a meaningful order, but the gaps need not be equal.
cards.takeaway: Ranking does not establish numerical distance.

cards.title: Which summaries make sense for a nominal variable?
cards.answer: Counts, proportions, and the mode.
cards.takeaway: Averaging arbitrary category codes has no stable meaning.

cards.title: Why be cautious about averaging ordinal scores?
cards.answer: A mean treats numerical gaps as meaningful and equal, which the category order alone does not justify.
cards.takeaway: An encoding can silently add assumptions.

cards.title: How do you calculate a sample mean?
cards.answer: Add all n values and divide by n.
cards.takeaway: Every observation contributes equally to the sum.

cards.title: How do you calculate the median of an even number of numeric values?
cards.answer: Sort the values and average the two middle ones.
cards.takeaway: The median locates the center by position.

cards.title: Which moves more when one value becomes extremely large: mean or median?
cards.answer: Usually the mean; the median depends on order rather than the extreme value's distance.
cards.takeaway: The mean is sensitive to magnitude.

cards.title: Which tail names a right-skewed distribution?
cards.answer: The long right tail, even if most observations are on the left.
cards.takeaway: Skew is named for the tail, not the crowded side.

cards.title: What is the range of 2, 5, 7, and 12?
cards.takeaway: The range uses only the two extremes.

cards.title: What is the usual unbiased sample variance for IID data?
cards.takeaway: Estimating the mean uses one degree of freedom.

cards.title: Why is standard deviation easier to interpret than variance?
cards.answer: It has the original measurement units; variance has squared units.
cards.takeaway: Taking a square root restores the measurement scale.

cards.title: What does a variable's distribution describe?
cards.answer: Which values occur and how frequently they occur.
cards.takeaway: A center alone leaves out the shape and spread.

cards.title: Why is skewness meaningless for unordered categories?
cards.answer: Their horizontal order can be rearranged arbitrarily.
cards.takeaway: A tail requires a meaningful direction.

cards.title: How do CSV and JSON typically differ structurally?
cards.answer: CSV is a rectangular table; JSON can represent nested records with differing fields.
cards.takeaway: A collection of records is not always analysis-ready rows.

cards.title: What should one row represent in a tidy table?
cards.answer: One observation of a clearly defined unit.
cards.takeaway: Decide what is being observed before counting rows.

cards.title: What should one column represent in a tidy table?
cards.answer: One variable measured consistently across observations.
cards.takeaway: Mixing meanings in one column makes analysis ambiguous.

cards.title: Can cleaning repair a dataset that lacks the information needed for the question?
cards.answer: No. Better formatting cannot create missing study design or relevant measurements.
cards.takeaway: Sometimes the right next step is different data.

cards.title: Why turn date-valued column headers into a date column?
cards.answer: Dates are values of a variable. Long form stores them as values and can append new observations consistently.
cards.takeaway: Headers should name variables, not enumerate their possible values.

cards.title: Why split a cell containing both a measurement and a unit?
cards.answer: They are separate pieces of information needed for consistent interpretation and conversion.
cards.takeaway: One cell should not hide several variables.

cards.title: Why separate person records from repeated event records?
cards.answer: They represent different observation units; mixing them duplicates person attributes and can distort counts.
cards.takeaway: One kind of record per table clarifies what a row means.

cards.title: How does a sample differ from a population?
cards.answer: The population is the full target group; the sample contains the observations actually collected.
cards.takeaway: The sample is evidence about a larger target, not automatically its mirror.

cards.title: What is selection bias?
cards.answer: The selection process systematically favors some relevant kinds of observations over others.
cards.takeaway: More data from a biased process can preserve the bias.

cards.title: How can nonresponse distort a survey?
cards.answer: People who respond may differ systematically from those who do not.
cards.takeaway: The missing voices may be relevant to the answer.

cards.title: Why is a sample mean uncertain even when calculated exactly?
cards.answer: A different sample would generally give a different mean.
cards.takeaway: Computational precision does not remove sampling variation.

cards.title: What is the median of 17, 19, 21, 22, 23, 23, 23, 38?
cards.answer: 22.5, the average of 22 and 23.
cards.takeaway: Use the middle positions after sorting.

cards.title: Why does variance react strongly to outliers?
cards.answer: It squares deviations, giving large distances disproportionately large contributions.
cards.takeaway: Twice the deviation produces four times the squared contribution.

cards.title: What does Pearson correlation measure?
cards.answer: The strength and direction of a linear relationship between two varying quantitative variables.
cards.takeaway: It summarizes linear association, not every kind of dependence.

cards.title: What values can Pearson correlation take?
cards.answer: From −1 to 1, provided both variables have nonzero variance.
cards.takeaway: The sign gives direction; magnitude gives linear strength.

cards.title: Does converting meters to centimeters change Pearson correlation?
cards.answer: No. Positive linear rescaling leaves it unchanged.
cards.takeaway: Standardization removes measurement units.

cards.title: Does an observed correlation establish a causal effect?
cards.answer: No. Confounding, selection, or other mechanisms can produce association.
cards.takeaway: A predictive relationship is not automatically an intervention effect.

cards.title: Does correlation near zero prove no relationship?
cards.answer: No. A strong curved or symmetric nonlinear relationship can have zero linear correlation.
cards.takeaway: Always look beyond a single number.

cards.title: What lesson does Anscombe's quartet teach?
cards.answer: Datasets can share common summary statistics while having very different shapes and outliers.
cards.takeaway: Plot the data before trusting summaries alone.

cards.title: What is exploratory data analysis for?
cards.answer: Finding patterns, problems, and useful questions through summaries and visual inspection.
cards.takeaway: Exploration helps decide what to model and what to check.

cards.title: What should guide the choice of a chart?
cards.answer: The variable types and whether you want to show distribution, relationship, composition, or comparison.
cards.takeaway: Choose the display to answer a question.

cards.title: What does a histogram show?
cards.answer: How numerical observations are distributed across intervals.
cards.takeaway: Bins group nearby values to reveal distribution shape.

cards.title: Why examine more than one histogram bin width?
cards.answer: Bin choices can hide or exaggerate apparent peaks and gaps.
cards.takeaway: A pattern should not depend entirely on one arbitrary setting.

cards.title: When is a bar chart more appropriate than a histogram?
cards.answer: When comparing categories rather than intervals on a numeric scale.
cards.takeaway: Categories and numeric bins represent different structures.

cards.title: Why are bars often easier to compare than pie slices?
cards.answer: Aligned lengths are easier to compare accurately than angles or areas.
cards.takeaway: Use an encoding that makes the comparison easy.

cards.title: Which plot is a natural starting point for two quantitative variables?
cards.answer: A scatter plot with one variable on each axis.
cards.takeaway: Each point preserves an observation's paired values.

cards.title: What does a stacked area chart emphasize?
cards.answer: How a total and its subgroup composition change over a continuous axis such as time.
cards.takeaway: Middle layers lack a common baseline, making precise comparisons harder.

cards.title: Why overlay or align distributions from different groups?
cards.answer: To compare their centers, spread, and shapes.
cards.takeaway: Similar averages can hide different distributions.

cards.title: What does the box in a standard boxplot represent?
cards.answer: The middle 50% of observations, from the first to third quartile, with a median line.
cards.takeaway: The box summarizes spread around the center.

cards.title: Does a point beyond a boxplot whisker automatically mean bad data?
cards.answer: No. It is unusual under the plotting rule and deserves investigation.
cards.takeaway: A flag is not proof of a recording error.

cards.title: What extra information can a violin plot show compared with a boxplot?
cards.answer: An estimated distribution shape, including possible multiple peaks.
cards.takeaway: Its shape also depends on density-smoothing choices.

cards.title: How can a scatter plot include a third categorical variable?
cards.answer: Use color, marker shape, or separate panels for categories.
cards.takeaway: Add an encoding only when it helps interpretation.

cards.title: Why can plotting every feature at once become unhelpful?
cards.answer: Overlapping marks and competing encodings can obscure the relationships you want to see.
cards.takeaway: More displayed information can mean less usable information.

cards.title: What does coloring a pair plot by species help reveal?
cards.answer: Whether apparent relationships differ across species or arise from mixing groups.
cards.takeaway: Group structure can explain an overall pattern.

cards.title: What does graphical integrity require?
cards.answer: Representing magnitudes, scales, and context honestly rather than exaggerating a preferred message.
cards.takeaway: The chart should preserve the meaning of the data.

cards.title: Why remove decorative elements that do not convey information?
cards.answer: They compete with the evidence for attention.
cards.takeaway: A reader should see the pattern before the decoration.

cards.title: When is a diverging color scale useful?
cards.answer: When values extend on both sides of a meaningful center, such as positive and negative deviations from zero.
cards.takeaway: The midpoint anchors two directions of change.

cards.title: What kind of colors suit unordered categories?
cards.answer: Distinct colors without implying a numerical ranking.
cards.takeaway: Different categories need distinction, not an artificial gradient.

cards.title: What kind of color scale suits ordered values?
cards.answer: A perceptually ordered scale, often varying lightness.
cards.takeaway: The visual order should match the data order.

cards.title: Why avoid relying only on red-versus-green differences?
cards.answer: Some readers cannot reliably distinguish them. Add labels, shapes, or other cues.
cards.takeaway: Color should reinforce meaning rather than be its only carrier.

cards.title: Why adapt a visualization to its audience?
cards.answer: Their knowledge and decision needs determine which labels, context, and detail are useful.
cards.takeaway: A technically correct chart still needs to communicate.

cards.title: In a model predicting house prices from size and location, which quantity is y?
cards.answer: The house price: the outcome you want to predict. It is also called the response or target; size and location are predictors.
cards.takeaway: The target determines what counts as a correct prediction.

cards.title: What are predictors or features?
cards.answer: The input variables used to predict the response.
cards.takeaway: A useful feature must be available when the prediction is made.

cards.title: What is the shape of a design matrix with n observations and p input features?
cards.answer: n rows by p columns, before adding any explicit intercept column.
cards.takeaway: Rows are cases; columns are features.

cards.title: Why keep a single feature as an \(n\times 1\) matrix for model fitting?
cards.answer: The estimator expects a collection of rows and feature columns, even when there is only one feature.
cards.takeaway: One feature is still a feature axis.

cards.title: How do df['x'] and df[['x']] differ?
cards.answer: For a unique column name, the first returns a Series; the second returns a one-column DataFrame.
cards.takeaway: Double brackets preserve a two-dimensional feature table.

cards.title: What do f(X) and \(\varepsilon\) represent in \(y=f(X)+\varepsilon\)?
cards.answer: f(X) is the underlying systematic relationship; \(\varepsilon\) is the remaining random variation.
cards.takeaway: A model estimates signal from noisy observations.

cards.title: How do inference and prediction emphasize different goals?
cards.answer: Inference emphasizes understanding relationships; prediction emphasizes accuracy on new observations.
cards.takeaway: The goal affects how you judge a model.

cards.title: What does 1-NN predict at a unique training input?
cards.answer: Its own observed response, assuming that observation is included among candidates.
cards.takeaway: Perfect training fit can simply mean memorization.

cards.title: Why does k-nearest-neighbors keep the training observations for prediction?
cards.answer: It predicts from nearby stored examples instead of compressing the relationship into a fixed-size coefficient formula. This is why it is called nonparametric; it still has choices such as the number of neighbors.
cards.takeaway: Nonparametric does not mean assumption-free.

cards.title: How does kNN regression predict at a new input?
cards.answer: Find its k nearest training inputs and average their response values.
cards.takeaway: Nearby examples supply a local estimate.

cards.title: If the three nearest responses are 4, 7, and 10, what does unweighted 3-NN predict?
cards.takeaway: Regression averages responses rather than taking a category vote.

cards.title: Why is k a hyperparameter?
cards.answer: It is chosen to configure the learning procedure rather than fitted as a regression coefficient.
cards.takeaway: Tune the neighborhood size using held-out performance.

cards.title: What are the roles of training, validation, and test data?
cards.answer: Training fits the model; validation chooses settings; test data assess the finalized procedure.
cards.takeaway: Do not use the final exam to choose the answers.

cards.title: What is a residual when \(y=10\) and \(\hat{y}=7\)?
cards.answer: \(y-\hat{y}=3\), indicating underprediction.
cards.takeaway: Keep the sign when diagnosing the direction of errors.

cards.title: How is mean squared error calculated?
cards.answer: Average the squared residuals: \(\operatorname{MSE}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_i(y_i-\hat y_i)^2\).
cards.takeaway: Squaring prevents positive and negative errors from cancelling.

cards.title: What is the MSE for residuals −2, 0, and 4?
cards.takeaway: Square first, then average.

cards.title: Why report RMSE instead of MSE for interpretability?
cards.answer: RMSE is \(\sqrt{\operatorname{MSE}}\) and has the same units as the response.
cards.takeaway: The result can be compared directly with the measurement scale.

cards.title: How does MAE treat large errors differently from MSE?
cards.answer: MAE grows linearly with error magnitude; MSE grows quadratically.
cards.takeaway: MSE gives extreme misses more influence.

cards.title: Is MSE the best loss for every application?
cards.answer: No. Choose a loss that reflects the consequences of different errors.
cards.takeaway: The definition of “best” is part of the problem.

cards.title: Why be cautious when two k values have nearly equal validation MSE?
cards.answer: A different split may reverse their ranking.
cards.takeaway: A small observed difference may be sampling variation.

cards.title: If responses and predictions are multiplied by 10, what happens to MSE?
cards.answer: It is multiplied by 100.
cards.takeaway: Squared errors have squared units.

cards.title: How is the usual \(R^{2}\) score defined?
cards.answer: \(1-\frac{\sum_i(y_i-\hat y_i)^2}{\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2}\), when the denominator is positive.
cards.takeaway: It compares error with a mean-only benchmark on the evaluated observations.

cards.title: What does \(R^{2}=0\) mean?
cards.answer: The model matches the squared error of the evaluated data's mean benchmark.
cards.takeaway: Zero improvement is not necessarily zero error.

cards.title: What does \(R^{2}=1\) mean on an evaluated dataset?
cards.answer: All its predictions match the observed responses exactly, assuming nonconstant responses.
cards.takeaway: A perfect score on training data does not establish generalization.

cards.title: Why isn't predicting the mean the worst possible model?
cards.answer: Other predictions can have arbitrarily larger errors and therefore negative \(R^{2}\).
cards.takeaway: The mean is a reference baseline, not a lower performance bound.

cards.title: What happens when k equals the entire training-set size?
cards.answer: Every prediction is the training response mean.
cards.takeaway: The neighborhood no longer depends on the query.

cards.title: How does increasing k usually change a kNN regression curve?
cards.answer: It makes the curve smoother by averaging more observations.
cards.takeaway: Smoothing reduces sensitivity but can wash out local structure.

cards.title: What is Euclidean distance between vectors x and z?
cards.answer: \(\sqrt{\sum_j(x_j-z_j)^2}\).
cards.takeaway: Differences in every feature contribute to closeness.

cards.title: What is the Euclidean distance between (0,0) and (3,4)?
cards.answer: 5, because \(\sqrt{9+16}=5\).
cards.takeaway: Distance combines coordinate differences geometrically.

cards.title: Why scale features before distance-based modeling?
cards.answer: A feature with large numerical units can dominate distances even when it is not more informative.
cards.takeaway: Measurement units should not silently decide the neighbors.

cards.title: Why does kNN become difficult in high dimensions?
cards.answer: Data become sparse, so nearby observations may no longer be truly local or clearly distinguishable.
cards.takeaway: A useful neighborhood needs enough data in the relevant space.

cards.title: What is the prediction equation for simple linear regression?
cards.answer: \(\hat{y}=\hat{\beta}_{0}+\hat{\beta}_{1}x\).
cards.takeaway: One intercept and one slope define the fitted line.

cards.title: What does ordinary least squares choose?
cards.answer: Coefficients that minimize the sum, or equivalently the mean, of squared training residuals.
cards.takeaway: Training is an optimization problem.

cards.title: If \(\hat{y}=7+0.05x\), what is the prediction at \(x=100\)?
cards.takeaway: Substitute the input into the fitted equation.

cards.title: What does a partial derivative hold fixed?
cards.answer: All the other arguments while varying the chosen one.
cards.takeaway: It isolates sensitivity to one coefficient.

cards.title: For \(r=y-\beta _{0}-\beta _{1}x\), what is \(\partial r^{2}/\partial \beta _{0}\)?
cards.takeaway: Increasing the intercept decreases the residual.

cards.title: For \(r=y-\beta _{0}-\beta _{1}x\), what is \(\partial r^{2}/\partial \beta _{1}\)?
cards.answer: −2xr.
cards.takeaway: The input scales how strongly a slope change affects the prediction.

cards.title: Does a zero gradient always identify a minimum?
cards.answer: No. In general it can also identify a maximum or saddle; convex least squares makes stationary points global minima.
cards.takeaway: Stationarity needs the shape of the objective for interpretation.

cards.title: How does the gradient tell an optimizer which way to change its parameters?
cards.answer: It collects the partial derivatives of the loss. Locally it points toward the steepest increase; a small step in the opposite direction decreases a differentiable loss when the gradient is nonzero.
cards.takeaway: It collects local changes in every coefficient direction.

cards.title: What is the fitted simple-regression slope with an intercept?
cards.answer: \(\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)}{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2}\), provided x varies.
cards.takeaway: The slope compares joint variation with predictor variation.

cards.title: How do you recover the fitted intercept from the slope?
cards.answer: \(\hat{\beta}_{0}=\bar{y}-\hat{\beta}_{1}\bar{x}\).
cards.takeaway: The fitted line passes through the sample means.

cards.title: Why can't simple regression identify a unique slope when all x values are equal?
cards.answer: There is no predictor variation; changes in slope can be offset by the intercept.
cards.takeaway: The data need different x values to learn a change with x.

cards.title: What does multiple linear regression add to simple regression?
cards.answer: Several predictor terms: \(\hat{y}=\hat{\beta}_{0}+\sum _{j}\hat{\beta}_{j}x_{j}\).
cards.takeaway: Each coefficient describes a contribution conditional on the others.

cards.title: What does a column of ones represent in the design matrix?
cards.answer: The intercept term.
cards.takeaway: Multiplying a coefficient by 1 adds the same offset to every row.

cards.title: With n observations, p predictors, and an explicit intercept, how many columns does X have?
cards.takeaway: Count the intercept among the fitted coefficients.

cards.title: What is the squared-error loss in matrix notation?
cards.answer: \(\Vert y-X\beta \Vert ^{2}=(y-X\beta )^{\mathsf{T}}(y-X\beta )\).
cards.takeaway: The residual vector's squared length sums all squared errors.

cards.title: Does dividing squared-error loss by n change the unregularized minimizer?
cards.answer: No. Multiplying an objective by a positive constant preserves its minimizers.
cards.takeaway: The scale of the objective differs from the location of its minimum.

cards.title: What is the gradient of \(\Vert y-X\beta \Vert ^{2}\) with respect to \(\beta\)?
cards.answer: \(-2X^{\mathsf{T}}(y-X\beta )\).
cards.takeaway: A stationary fit has no residual component along a design column.

cards.title: What equations characterize an ordinary least-squares solution?
cards.answer: \(X^{\mathsf{T}}X\hat{\beta}=X^{\mathsf{T}}y\).
cards.takeaway: The residual is orthogonal to every available predictor direction.

cards.title: When is \(\hat{\beta}=(X^{\mathsf{T}}X)^{-1}X^{\mathsf{T}}y\) valid?
cards.answer: When X has full column rank, so \(X^{\mathsf{T}}X\) is invertible.
cards.takeaway: Writing an inverse does not guarantee it exists.

cards.title: What does the intercept represent?
cards.answer: The predicted response when all numeric predictors are zero and categorical predictors are at their reference levels.
cards.takeaway: Its practical meaning depends on whether that setting is realistic.

cards.title: In \(\hat{y}=5+3x\), what does the slope 3 mean?
cards.answer: The predicted response increases by 3 units for a one-unit increase in x.
cards.takeaway: A coefficient connects changes on two measurement scales.

cards.title: What does a multiple-regression slope describe without interactions?
cards.answer: The predicted response change for a one-unit predictor increase, holding other predictors fixed.
cards.takeaway: It is a conditional association, not necessarily a causal effect.

cards.title: Why can't raw coefficient magnitudes reliably rank feature importance?
cards.answer: Features measured on different scales produce coefficients in different units.
cards.takeaway: A small coefficient can multiply a very large input scale.

cards.title: How do you standardize a varying feature?
cards.answer: Subtract its training mean and divide by its training standard deviation.
cards.takeaway: A one-unit change then represents one training standard deviation.

cards.title: How does min–max scaling transform a nonconstant feature?
cards.answer: Use (x−minimum)/(maximum−minimum), with extrema learned from training data.
cards.takeaway: The training range becomes 0 to 1.

cards.title: Does standardization make a variable normally distributed?
cards.answer: No. It changes location and scale, not the underlying shape.
cards.takeaway: Zero mean and unit variance do not imply a bell curve.

cards.title: Why does strong collinearity make coefficient interpretation difficult?
cards.answer: Predictors share information, so their separate contributions are hard to distinguish and estimates can be unstable.
cards.takeaway: Stable predictions can coexist with unstable coefficients.

cards.title: How do exact and near collinearity differ for coefficient uniqueness?
cards.answer: Exact dependence can make OLS coefficients nonunique; near dependence can make a unique solution highly sensitive.
cards.takeaway: Nonunique and unstable are related but different problems.

cards.title: What does a 0/1 indicator encode?
cards.answer: Whether an observation belongs to a specified group.
cards.takeaway: A category becomes a usable design column.

cards.title: In \(\hat{y}=\beta _{0}+\beta _{1}D\), what is the predicted group difference?
cards.answer: \(\beta _{1}\): the prediction at \(D=1\) minus the prediction at \(D=0\).
cards.takeaway: The intercept is the reference-group prediction.

cards.title: With an intercept, how many ordinary dummy columns represent K categories without redundancy?
cards.answer: K−1, with one reference category.
cards.takeaway: All K indicators already sum to the intercept column.

cards.title: Does changing the reference category change the fitted predictions?
cards.answer: No, when it is an equivalent recoding of the same model.
cards.takeaway: The coefficient interpretation changes, not the model space.

cards.title: Must errors be normal to compute an OLS fit?
cards.answer: No. Normality is used for certain exact inferential results, not for minimizing squared error.
cards.takeaway: Fitting a model and justifying inference require different assumptions.

cards.title: Are model errors and fitted residuals the same thing?
cards.answer: No. Errors use the unknown true mean; residuals use an estimated mean and are generally correlated after fitting.
cards.takeaway: Estimated deviations inherit constraints from the fit.

cards.title: Why plot residuals against fitted values in multiple regression?
cards.answer: It can reveal curvature or changing spread without choosing only one predictor axis.
cards.takeaway: Residual patterns show what the fit leaves unexplained.

cards.title: Why might a model fit its training data closely but predict new data poorly?
cards.answer: It may have learned sample-specific noise instead of a pattern that persists. This is overfitting; performance on suitable held-out data helps reveal it.
cards.takeaway: The training sample is not the entire prediction problem.

cards.title: What does an interaction term let a regression model express?
cards.answer: The effect of one predictor can depend on another predictor's value.
cards.takeaway: One universal slope may not describe every context.

cards.title: In \(f=\beta _{0}+\beta _{1}x+\beta _{2}z+\beta _{3}xz\), what is the slope with respect to x?
cards.takeaway: The interaction makes the x effect depend on z.

cards.title: What do a numeric predictor and a group indicator produce without an interaction?
cards.answer: Group-specific intercepts with the same slope.
cards.takeaway: The fitted lines are parallel.

cards.title: How does adding xD change the group lines when D is 0 or 1?
cards.answer: Their slopes can differ: \(\beta _{1}\) for \(D=0\) and \(\beta _{1}+\beta _{3}\) for \(D=1\).
cards.takeaway: The interaction coefficient is the slope difference.

cards.title: If \(\beta _{1}=2\) and \(\beta _{3}=-0.5\), what is the x slope for \(D=1\)?
cards.takeaway: Add the interaction adjustment to the baseline slope.

cards.title: Why is polynomial regression still linear regression?
cards.answer: It is linear in the unknown coefficients, even though it is nonlinear in x.
cards.takeaway: Linear describes the parameters, not necessarily the plotted curve.

cards.title: How many coefficients does a one-variable degree-M polynomial have with an intercept?
cards.takeaway: The constant term counts as a coefficient too.

cards.title: What is a quadratic design row for an input x?
cards.takeaway: Transform the input, then fit ordinary linear coefficients.

cards.title: What is the cubic design row at \(x=2\)?
cards.takeaway: Each additional column is another power of the same input.

cards.title: Why inspect the columns produced by polynomial feature expansion?
cards.answer: With several inputs, it may add interaction terms as well as individual powers.
cards.takeaway: Feature expansion can create more terms than you intended.

cards.title: Why avoid both an explicit all-ones feature and a redundant fitted intercept?
cards.answer: They represent the same constant direction and create redundant parameters.
cards.takeaway: Choose one consistent intercept convention.

cards.title: Why can an overly simple model perform poorly even on its training data?
cards.answer: It cannot express an important pattern in the data. This is underfitting; collecting more data alone does not fix a model that is too restricted.
cards.takeaway: Even excellent optimization cannot fix the wrong model family.

cards.title: Why can high polynomial powers cause numerical trouble?
cards.answer: Very large or tiny input values become extreme when raised to high powers.
cards.takeaway: Scale can make a mathematically valid model difficult to compute reliably.

cards.title: Why inspect model predictions even if MSE is small?
cards.answer: The model may imply implausible responses or relationships in important parts of the input range.
cards.takeaway: One aggregate score can hide consequential failures.

cards.title: What should improve if a model has learned a useful pattern rather than memorized its sample?
cards.answer: Its predictions on relevant new observations. This ability to transfer beyond the training data is called generalization.
cards.takeaway: New-data performance is the goal, not training perfection.

cards.title: Why not pick hyperparameters using test-set performance?
cards.answer: The selection would adapt to the test data, making its final score optimistically biased.
cards.takeaway: An untouched test set evaluates the completed choice.

cards.title: How many predictor subsets exist for J candidate predictors?
cards.answer: \(2^{J}\), including the empty subset.
cards.takeaway: Each predictor has two choices: include or exclude.

cards.title: How many subsets can be formed from 5 predictors?
cards.takeaway: Exhaustive search grows exponentially.

cards.title: How does forward selection build a model?
cards.answer: Start with no predictors and repeatedly add the candidate that best improves the chosen evaluation criterion.
cards.takeaway: It builds one path rather than checking every subset.

cards.title: Does forward selection guarantee the globally best predictor subset?
cards.answer: No. An early greedy choice can exclude better combinations from the path.
cards.takeaway: A computational shortcut can miss joint effects.

cards.title: How many candidate additions are checked along a full forward-selection path with J predictors?
cards.answer: \(J+(J-1)+\cdots +1=J(J+1)/2\), excluding the initial null model.
cards.takeaway: The number of candidate fits grows quadratically rather than exponentially.

cards.title: How do polynomial coefficients differ from polynomial degree?
cards.answer: Coefficients are fitted parameters; degree is a hyperparameter selecting the model's form.
cards.takeaway: Configuration choices sit outside a single model fit.

cards.title: What does low training error but much higher validation error suggest?
cards.answer: Overfitting, assuming both sets represent the same prediction setting.
cards.takeaway: Training success is not transferring to held-out data.

cards.title: What can high training and validation errors suggest?
cards.answer: Underfitting or a noisy/difficult prediction problem.
cards.takeaway: High error alone does not identify its cause.

cards.title: Why can model choice be fragile with one validation split?
cards.answer: Its particular observations can accidentally favor one model over another.
cards.takeaway: The split itself adds uncertainty.

cards.title: Can repeated tuning overfit cross-validation results?
cards.answer: Yes. Trying many choices can adapt to the validation evidence.
cards.takeaway: Cross-validation reduces split dependence, not every form of selection bias.

cards.title: Does cross-validation replace the final untouched test set?
cards.answer: No, when CV is used to choose the model; the test set still evaluates the finalized choice.
cards.takeaway: Selection and final evaluation remain separate roles.

cards.title: If three equal-sized folds have MSEs 2, 4, and 6, what is their mean CV MSE?
cards.takeaway: Aggregate held-out performance across splits.

cards.title: How does K-fold cross-validation work?
cards.answer: Split development data into K folds, fit on K−1 folds, validate on the remaining fold, and rotate.
cards.takeaway: Every observation gets a turn as held-out data.

cards.title: How many fits are needed for one candidate in 5-fold CV?
cards.answer: Five, before any final refit.
cards.takeaway: Each validation fold needs a model trained without it.

cards.title: Where should learned scaling or imputation be fitted during CV?
cards.answer: Inside each training fold, then applied to its validation fold.
cards.takeaway: Validation data should not influence preprocessing estimates.

cards.title: What is leave-one-out cross-validation?
cards.answer: Use each observation alone as validation and train on all the others.
cards.takeaway: It is K-fold CV with K equal to the sample size.

cards.title: Why can leave-one-out CV be expensive?
cards.answer: It usually requires one fit per observation.
cards.takeaway: Using almost all data per fit can increase computational cost.

cards.title: Why does a cross-validation scorer sometimes return negative MSE?
cards.answer: The scoring convention maximizes values, so it negates a loss that should be minimized.
cards.takeaway: A score of −2 is better than −5 for negative MSE.

cards.title: If you knew the true expected response for each input, would prediction error disappear?
cards.answer: Not if individual responses still vary around that expected value. This remaining variation is irreducible noise for the available predictors and setting.
cards.takeaway: Better fitting cannot predict randomness absent from the inputs.

cards.title: Which part of prediction error can a better model or more informative training data reduce?
cards.answer: The error from an inadequate relationship or imperfect estimation of it. This is reducible error, distinct from unpredictable variation around the true expected response.
cards.takeaway: Better models or better estimation may reduce it.

cards.title: What does model variance measure at a fixed x?
cards.answer: How predictions change across repeated training samples.
cards.takeaway: A high-variance model reacts strongly to the particular data collected.

cards.title: What does it mean if repeated fits systematically predict above the true mean at an input?
cards.answer: They have positive prediction bias there: the average prediction across training samples exceeds the true expected response f(x). Bias describes systematic error, not the spread between fits.
cards.takeaway: Bias concerns systematic error across possible fits.

cards.title: What are the usual components of expected squared prediction error?
cards.answer: Squared bias, model variance, and irreducible noise variance, under the standard zero-mean noise setup.
cards.takeaway: Reducing one component does not necessarily reduce the total.

cards.title: How does increasing flexibility often affect bias and variance?
cards.answer: It can lower bias while increasing variance.
cards.takeaway: More adaptable models can also be less stable.

cards.title: Can a biased estimator predict better than an unbiased one?
cards.answer: Yes, if its variance reduction outweighs the added squared bias.
cards.takeaway: Prediction error balances both components.

cards.title: What does regularized regression optimize?
cards.answer: A data-fit loss plus a coefficient penalty weighted by \(\lambda\).
cards.takeaway: A good fit must also pay for complexity.

cards.title: What happens when \(\lambda =0\) in ridge or lasso?
cards.answer: The penalty disappears, leaving ordinary least squares.
cards.takeaway: Zero regularization returns to the original fitting objective.

cards.title: What happens to penalized slopes as \(\lambda\) becomes very large?
cards.answer: They shrink toward zero; an unpenalized intercept can remain.
cards.takeaway: Very strong regularization approaches a constant predictor.

cards.title: Can regularization be too strong?
cards.answer: Yes. Excessive shrinkage can erase useful signal and underfit.
cards.takeaway: Regularization strength needs tuning rather than maximization.

cards.title: How should prediction-focused regularization strength be chosen?
cards.answer: Compare candidate \(\lambda\) values using validation or cross-validation loss.
cards.takeaway: The penalty's training value does not measure held-out usefulness.

cards.title: What coefficient penalty does lasso use?
cards.answer: The L1 penalty \(\lambda\sum_j|\beta_j|\), usually excluding the intercept.
cards.takeaway: Absolute values create a sharp corner at zero.

cards.title: What coefficient penalty does ridge use?
cards.answer: The squared L2 penalty \(\lambda\sum_j\beta_j^2\), usually excluding the intercept.
cards.takeaway: Large coefficients become increasingly expensive.

cards.title: Why standardize predictors before applying comparable slope penalties?
cards.answer: Changing a feature's units changes the coefficient needed for the same prediction and therefore its penalty.
cards.takeaway: Unscaled penalties can treat units as importance.

cards.title: Why is the intercept usually left unpenalized?
cards.answer: It sets the overall response level rather than a feature effect.
cards.takeaway: Shifting the response's origin should not change how slopes are penalized.

cards.title: For centered data and loss \(\Vert y-X\beta \Vert ^{2}+\lambda \Vert \beta \Vert ^{2}\), what is the ridge solution?
cards.answer: \(\hat{\beta}=(X^{\mathsf{T}}X+\lambda I)^{-1}X^{\mathsf{T}}y\) for \(\lambda >0\).
cards.takeaway: Adding \(\lambda\) stabilizes weak coefficient directions.

cards.title: Why is \(X^{\mathsf{T}}X+\lambda I\) invertible when \(\lambda >0\)?
cards.answer: For nonzero v, \(v^{\mathsf{T}}(X^{\mathsf{T}}X+\lambda I)v=\Vert Xv\Vert ^{2}+\lambda \Vert v\Vert ^{2}>0\).
cards.takeaway: The penalty removes flat directions in the slope objective.

cards.title: If the fit loss is MSE rather than SSE, does the same numerical \(\lambda\) mean the same penalty strength?
cards.answer: No. With \(\operatorname{MSE}+\lambda \Vert \beta \Vert ^{2}\), the normal equations contain \(X^{\mathsf{T}}X+n\lambda I\).
cards.takeaway: Always match \(\lambda\) to the objective's scaling convention.

cards.title: Why try \(\lambda\) values spread across orders of magnitude?
cards.answer: Useful strengths can differ by factors of ten or more.
cards.takeaway: A logarithmic grid explores weak and strong penalties efficiently.

cards.title: Can you reuse one fitted coefficient vector for every candidate \(\lambda\)?
cards.answer: No. Each \(\lambda\) defines a different optimization problem and generally needs its own fit.
cards.takeaway: Tuning changes the model, not only its score.

cards.title: Should validation MSE include the training coefficient penalty?
cards.answer: No. Use prediction error on held-out observations to compare predictive performance.
cards.takeaway: The penalty guides fitting; validation judges the resulting predictions.

cards.title: After selecting \(\lambda\), what data can you use for the final refit?
cards.answer: All development data previously used for training and validation, keeping the test set untouched.
cards.takeaway: Once the setting is fixed, use available development information.

cards.title: With 10 \(\lambda\) values and 5 CV folds, how many candidate fits are needed?
cards.answer: 50, plus the final refit.
cards.takeaway: Every setting must be evaluated across the same fold structure.

cards.title: Why is lasso optimization less direct than solving ridge's linear equations?
cards.answer: The absolute-value penalty is not differentiable at zero; algorithms handle that kink explicitly.
cards.takeaway: No derivative at zero does not mean no optimization solution.

cards.title: Which method can set coefficients exactly to zero: ridge or lasso?
cards.answer: Lasso commonly does; ridge generally shrinks coefficients continuously without selecting a sparse subset.
cards.takeaway: Shrinkage and feature selection are different outcomes.

cards.title: Why does lasso's constraint geometry favor zero coefficients?
cards.answer: Its corners lie on coordinate axes, where one or more coefficients are zero.
cards.takeaway: The penalty's shape helps determine the solution's structure.

cards.title: Why does ridge usually retain nonzero coefficients?
cards.answer: Its smooth constraint boundary does not favor axis-aligned corners.
cards.takeaway: A smooth penalty tends to distribute shrinkage.

cards.title: Why can ridge help with highly correlated predictors?
cards.answer: It stabilizes coefficient estimates by penalizing large solutions along weakly identified directions.
cards.takeaway: Accept some bias to reduce sensitivity.

cards.title: Does a zero lasso coefficient prove the predictor has no relationship with the response?
cards.answer: No. Selection depends on \(\lambda\), other predictors, and the sample.
cards.takeaway: A fitted exclusion is not a universal scientific conclusion.

cards.title: Why would repeated studies produce different regression coefficients?
cards.answer: The observed sample and noise vary, changing the fitted model.
cards.takeaway: A point estimate does not describe its own reliability.

cards.title: If you repeated a study many times, why would the fitted coefficient vary?
cards.answer: Each sample has different observations and noise. The distribution of coefficient estimates across those repeated samples is its sampling distribution.
cards.takeaway: One fitted coefficient is one realization of an estimator.

cards.title: In a bootstrap resample, can the same observation appear more than once?
cards.answer: Yes. Sampling with replacement keeps each observation eligible after every draw, so a resample can repeat some rows and omit others.
cards.takeaway: A bootstrap sample can repeat some records and omit others.

cards.title: How many observations are drawn for an ordinary size-n bootstrap replicate?
cards.answer: n draws with replacement from the original n observations.
cards.takeaway: Replicates preserve sample size, not the set of distinct rows.

cards.title: For pairs bootstrap in regression, what must be resampled together?
cards.answer: An entire observation row: its predictors and response.
cards.takeaway: Resampling X and y separately would destroy their relationship.

cards.title: What do you do after drawing each bootstrap dataset?
cards.answer: Refit the estimator and record the quantity of interest.
cards.takeaway: Variation across refits approximates sampling variation.

cards.title: How is a bootstrap standard error estimated?
cards.answer: Take the sample standard deviation of the statistic across bootstrap replicates.
cards.takeaway: Spread across refits estimates uncertainty in the statistic.

cards.title: Should the bootstrap SD of coefficients be divided by \(\sqrt{B}\) to estimate the coefficient's standard error?
cards.answer: No. The replicate SD already estimates that standard error; dividing by \(\sqrt{B}\) targets simulation averaging error instead.
cards.takeaway: More bootstrap runs do not create more observed data.

cards.title: What distribution does the ordinary nonparametric bootstrap sample from?
cards.answer: The empirical distribution placing equal mass on each observed record.
cards.takeaway: The observed sample stands in for the unknown population.

cards.title: What improves when you increase the number of bootstrap replicates B?
cards.answer: The numerical stability of the bootstrap estimate, not the information in the original dataset.
cards.takeaway: Reduce simulation noise without pretending to collect new observations.

cards.title: Can bootstrap resampling fix a biased or unrepresentative original sample?
cards.answer: No. It repeatedly reuses that sample's information and selection limitations.
cards.takeaway: Resampling does not repair the collection process.

cards.title: Why can ordinary row bootstrap fail for dependent observations?
cards.answer: Independent resampling breaks the dependence structure; a suitable design such as block resampling may be needed.
cards.takeaway: The resampling scheme must match the data structure.

cards.title: What does 95% confidence describe in frequentist inference?
cards.answer: The long-run coverage of the interval-building procedure under its assumptions.
cards.takeaway: The parameter is fixed; intervals vary across samples.

cards.title: Does a realized frequentist 95% CI assign 95% posterior probability to its parameter range?
cards.answer: No. That is a Bayesian probability statement requiring a posterior model.
cards.takeaway: Coverage and posterior probability answer different questions.

cards.title: How is a 95% percentile bootstrap interval constructed?
cards.answer: Use the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the bootstrap estimates.
cards.takeaway: Leave 2.5% of replicate estimates in each tail.

cards.title: If bootstrap percentiles are 1.2 and 3.8, what is the 95% percentile interval?
cards.takeaway: Report the endpoint values, not the percentile labels.

cards.title: When is estimate \(\pm\) roughly 2 standard errors a reasonable 95% interval approximation?
cards.answer: When the estimator's sampling distribution is approximately normal and the standard error estimate is suitable.
cards.takeaway: A symmetric interval may misrepresent a skewed distribution.

cards.title: In simple regression, how does predictor spread affect slope uncertainty?
cards.answer: Under equal-variance, uncorrelated errors, \(\operatorname{SE}(\hat\beta_1)=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2}}\).
cards.takeaway: A wider range of x provides more leverage for estimating a slope.

cards.title: If the error SD doubles while X stays fixed, what happens to coefficient standard errors?
cards.answer: They double under the same linear-model assumptions.
cards.takeaway: Noisier responses make the same design less informative.

cards.title: How is residual noise variance estimated in full-rank simple regression with an intercept?
cards.answer: \(s^2=\frac{\operatorname{SSE}}{n-2}\), for \(n>2\) under the usual model assumptions.
cards.takeaway: Two fitted coefficients use two degrees of freedom.

cards.title: Why isn't a large coefficient enough to establish statistical significance?
cards.answer: Its uncertainty and units matter; a large estimate can be imprecise.
cards.takeaway: Compare the signal with its uncertainty.

cards.title: What is the usual coefficient t statistic for testing \(\beta _{j}=0\)?
cards.answer: \(t=\hat{\beta}_{j}/\operatorname{SE}(\hat{\beta}_{j})\).
cards.takeaway: It measures how many standard errors the estimate lies from zero.

cards.title: If \(\hat{\beta}=0.6\) and its SE is 0.2, what is the t statistic for a zero null?
cards.takeaway: The same coefficient would provide less evidence with a larger SE.

cards.title: With p predictors and an intercept, what are the classical residual t-test degrees of freedom?
cards.answer: n−p−1 for a full-rank design under the normal linear model.
cards.takeaway: Count observations minus fitted coefficients.

cards.title: What assumptions justify the usual exact regression t reference distribution?
cards.answer: A correct linear mean, full-rank design, and independent Gaussian errors with constant variance, conditional on X.
cards.takeaway: The reference distribution depends on the model assumptions.

cards.title: Why use the absolute t statistic for a two-sided coefficient test?
cards.answer: Large departures in either the positive or negative direction count as evidence against zero.
cards.takeaway: Both tails matter when either sign is an alternative.

cards.title: If the null hypothesis were true, what question would a p-value answer?
cards.answer: How likely is a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed, under the null and model assumptions? It does not give the probability that the null itself is true.
cards.takeaway: It is a probability about possible data, conditional on a hypothesis.

cards.title: Does a p-value of 0.03 mean the null hypothesis has a 3% chance of being true?
cards.answer: No. It means results at least as extreme as observed have probability 3% under the null and model assumptions. Turning evidence into a probability about the hypothesis requires additional assumptions, such as a Bayesian model.
cards.takeaway: Do not reverse a conditional probability.

cards.title: Does a nonsignificant coefficient prove its effect is zero?
cards.answer: No. The data may be too imprecise to distinguish it from zero.
cards.takeaway: Absence of strong evidence is not proof of absence.

cards.title: Does a significant regression coefficient establish causation?
cards.answer: No. The regression can still reflect confounding or selection.
cards.takeaway: Statistical evidence for association is not an experimental intervention.

cards.title: Does statistical significance guarantee practical importance?
cards.answer: No. A tiny effect can be precisely estimated, and a meaningful effect can be uncertain.
cards.takeaway: Magnitude and uncertainty both matter.

cards.title: How can bootstrap fits give a confidence interval for the mean response at x?
cards.answer: Predict at the same x with each bootstrap fit and summarize those fitted mean predictions.
cards.takeaway: Parameter uncertainty becomes uncertainty about the mean curve.

cards.title: Why is a prediction interval usually wider than a confidence interval for the mean?
cards.answer: It includes both uncertainty in the fitted mean and variation of a new response around that mean.
cards.takeaway: Predicting one outcome is harder than estimating its average.

cards.title: Would knowing f(x) exactly remove all uncertainty in a new y?
cards.answer: No. The new response still contains random error \(\varepsilon\).
cards.takeaway: A perfectly known mean is not a perfectly predictable individual.

cards.title: What is missing if a bootstrap prediction interval uses only the fitted mean curves?
cards.answer: New-observation noise. A predictive simulation must also include suitable response variation.
cards.takeaway: A collection of fitted lines is a mean-uncertainty band.

cards.title: Under independent new noise, how do mean-estimation variance and response noise combine?
cards.answer: They add: \(\operatorname{Var}(\text{prediction error})=\operatorname{Var}(\text{estimated mean error})+\sigma^2\), under the model.
cards.takeaway: Uncertainty has two distinct sources.

cards.title: Move from 99 to 198: how does the binary64 spacing change?
cards.answer: It doubles, from \(2^{-46}\) to \(2^{-45}\). The exponent increases by one while binary64 keeps the same significand precision.
cards.takeaway: The floating-point grid stretches with scale.

cards.title: Which sequence sends the vector (1, 2) to (2, 2)?
cards.answer: A gives (2, 2). B first gives (2, 1), then (4, 1). Scaling and swapping generally do not commute.
cards.takeaway: Track the intermediate state rather than memorizing an order rule.
cards.source: PS1 · Q3 · companion practice · authored companion

cards.title: A map stretches one axis by 4 and the other by \(\frac{1}{4}\). What happens to area?
cards.answer: Area is unchanged because the product of singular values is 1. The shape can still become long and thin.
cards.takeaway: Shape distortion and area change are different quantities.
cards.source: PS1 · Q4 · companion practice · authored companion

cards.title: What is wrong with declaring this solution accurate from its residual alone?
cards.answer: The true solution is (1, 1), so the second component is entirely wrong. The tiny second diagonal entry hides that error in the residual.
cards.takeaway: An insensitive output direction can conceal a large solution error.
cards.source: Heath · §2.3.5, printed p. 61 · companion practice · authored companion

cards.title: If \(\kappa _{2}(X)=10^{4}\), which least-squares route forms a matrix with condition number \(10^{8}\)?
cards.answer: The normal equations form \(X^{\mathsf{T}}X\), whose 2-norm condition number is \(\kappa _{2}(X)^{2}\) \(=\) \(10^{8}\). QR avoids explicitly squaring the condition number.
cards.takeaway: Algebraically equivalent formulas can behave differently in finite precision.
cards.source: Heath · §3.3–3.5 · supporting least-squares reading · authored companion

cards.title: After factoring \(PA=LU\), what belongs in the missing solve step?
cards.answer: Solve \(Ux=y\) by back substitution. For each new right-hand side, reuse P, L, and U rather than refactoring A.
cards.takeaway: Pay for the factorization once, then solve cheaply.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 2 review · repeated systems · authored companion

cards.title: Which simulation budget halves the Monte Carlo standard error relative to N draws?
cards.answer: Budget B. Standard error scales as \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\), so quadrupling N halves it; doubling N only multiplies it by \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\).
cards.takeaway: Precision improves with the square root of computational effort.

cards.title: If a valid rejection envelope changes from \(M=2\) to \(M=8\), how does acceptance change?
cards.answer: Acceptance falls from \(\frac{1}{2}\) to \(\frac{1}{8}\). The looser envelope needs four times as many proposals per accepted draw on average.
cards.takeaway: A valid but loose bound wastes computation.

cards.title: Why is this Metropolis–Hastings output rule wrong?
cards.answer: Rejected proposals must append the current state again. Removing those repeated states changes residence times and generally changes the sampled distribution.
cards.takeaway: Staying put is part of the Markov chain.

items.label: Rule
items.value: Append a state only when a proposal is accepted

cards.title: Which proposal fails before you even inspect its importance weights?
cards.answer: B misses target mass outside [0,1]. A has full support, although its weight variance may still be poor.
cards.takeaway: Support is a necessary check, not a guarantee of efficiency.

visual.label: Target has positive density across the real line

cards.title: With a frozen reaction rate of 12 per second and \(\tau =0.25\) seconds, what count is sampled?
cards.answer: A Poisson random count with mean 3, not exactly three events. Freezing the reaction rate is the tau-leaping approximation.
cards.takeaway: The expected count is deterministic; the realized count is random.

cards.title: What posterior completes this coin-update sequence?
cards.answer: \(\operatorname{Beta}(5,8)\): add heads to the first shape parameter and tails to the second.
cards.takeaway: Conjugate updating turns evidence into parameter increments.

visual.label: Independent tosses with unknown head probability

cards.title: Do these coefficient pairs give different fitted values when \(X=\begin{bmatrix}x&x\end{bmatrix}\)?
cards.answer: No. Both give 3x because only the coefficient sum is identified. Individual coefficients differ, but their predictions agree.
cards.takeaway: Nonunique coordinates can describe the same fitted vector.
cards.source: HW2 · Q2 · companion practice · authored companion

cards.title: What condition is missing from this claim about an orthogonal projector?
cards.answer: For a real matrix, also require \(P^{\mathsf{T}}=P\). Idempotence alone describes a projection that may be oblique.
cards.takeaway: Projecting twice changes nothing; orthogonality additionally controls the direction.
cards.source: HW2 · Q5(a–c) · companion practice · authored companion

items.label: Claim
items.value: \(P^{2}\) \(=\) P, therefore P is an orthogonal projector

cards.title: If SSE stays 80 but \(\operatorname{rank}(X)\) rises from 4 to 10 with \(n=20\), what happens to \(s^{2}\)?
cards.answer: It rises from 5 to 8. With SSE held fixed, fewer residual degrees of freedom mean a larger variance estimate.
cards.takeaway: Fitting more independent directions leaves fewer directions for estimating noise.
cards.source: HW2 · Q7; least-squares theory · companion practice · authored companion

cards.title: Which independent measurement deserves four times the weight in WLS?
cards.answer: A. Inverse-variance weights are 1 and \(\frac{1}{4}\); the noisier measurement receives less influence.
