cards.takeaway: Precision, not variance, determines the weight.

cards.title: With \(s=2\) and mean-prediction leverage 0.25, which standard error is larger?
cards.answer: The new-response SE is \(\sqrt{5}\) \(\approx\) 2.24; the mean-response SE is 1. The extra 1 represents the new observation's noise.
cards.takeaway: Predicting an individual adds variability beyond estimating its mean.
cards.source: Inference notes · pp. 12–13 · companion practice · authored companion

cards.title: Why can this principal-components regression shortcut fail?
cards.answer: Predictor variance does not measure association with the response. A low-variance direction can carry important predictive signal, so discarding it can harm prediction.
cards.takeaway: PCA looks at X; prediction also needs the relationship with y.

items.label: Claim
items.value: The lowest-variance predictor direction cannot matter for prediction

cards.title: What is wrong with this plan for fixing a biased survey?
cards.answer: More responses can reduce random variation while leaving selection bias intact. Improve who can enter the sample, not just its size.
cards.takeaway: A precise answer about the wrong population is still misleading.

items.label: Plan
items.value: Keep the same selective recruitment method but collect ten times more responses

cards.title: If X is symmetric around zero and \(Y=X^{2}\), can Pearson correlation miss a perfect relationship?
cards.answer: Yes. The covariance is zero by symmetry, even though Y is completely determined by X. Pearson correlation measures linear association.
cards.takeaway: Zero linear association does not mean no relationship.

visual.label: Assume finite moments and nonzero variances

cards.title: Where does this model-selection workflow leak information?
cards.answer: Step 2 uses the test set for selection. Tune with validation data or cross-validation, then use the held-out test set for final evaluation.
cards.takeaway: A test set loses its independent role when it guides decisions.
cards.source: Lecture 4 · Part B · PDF p. 8 · authored companion

items.value: Choose the best using test-set MSE

cards.title: For \(f=1+2x+3z+4xz\), what happens to the x-slope when z changes from 0 to 1?
cards.answer: The slope changes from 2 to 6 because \(\partial f/\partial x=2+4z\).
cards.takeaway: An interaction makes one variable's effect depend on another.
cards.source: Lecture 6 · Part A · PDF p. 14 · authored companion

cards.title: Which penalty can produce exact zero coefficients and select features?
cards.answer: Lasso can set coefficients exactly to zero. Ridge generally shrinks them continuously without making them exactly zero.
cards.takeaway: The penalty's geometry changes the kind of solution favored.
cards.source: Lecture 7 · Part C · PDF p. 3 · authored companion

cards.title: Why does this resampling procedure fail to create an ordinary bootstrap distribution of the mean?
cards.answer: Each resample contains the same observations, so the mean never changes. An ordinary nonparametric bootstrap draws n observations with replacement.
cards.takeaway: Repeated and omitted observations create resampling variability.
cards.source: Lecture 8 · Part B · PDF p. 13 · authored companion

items.label: Procedure
items.value: Draw all n observations without replacement, then recompute the mean

cards.title: What crosses borders in international economics?
cards.answer: Goods and services, money, and investments. International economics studies how those cross-border interactions affect economies.
cards.takeaway: Trade and finance describe connected parts of the same system.

cards.title: How does international finance differ from international trade?
cards.answer: Trade focuses on goods and services crossing borders. Finance focuses on monetary transactions, financial claims, and the policies governing them.
cards.takeaway: A goods transaction often has a financial counterpart.

cards.title: Why measure trade relative to GDP rather than only in dollars?
cards.answer: The ratio indicates trade's importance relative to the economy's size. Dollar trade can rise simply because the whole economy grows.
cards.takeaway: Normalize before comparing economic exposure.

cards.title: Why can a large, diverse country have a lower trade-to-GDP ratio?
cards.answer: It can obtain more goods and resources within its own borders. Smaller economies often rely more heavily on foreign production and markets.
cards.takeaway: Economic size changes the need to cross borders.

cards.title: How can an international exchange benefit both sides?
cards.answer: Each party can receive something it values more than what it gives up. Differences in production opportunities create room for mutually beneficial exchange.
cards.takeaway: Trade is not automatically a zero-sum contest.

cards.title: Can a country gain from trade even if it is less productive in every good?
cards.answer: Yes. Gains depend on relative opportunity costs, not just absolute productivity. Specializing where its relative disadvantage is smallest can still improve its consumption possibilities.
cards.takeaway: Compare what production requires giving up.

cards.title: If you use scarce resources to produce one good, what is the economic cost beyond the money spent?
cards.answer: The best alternative production or activity you give up. This is opportunity cost: the trade-off created by using those resources here rather than elsewhere.
cards.takeaway: Scarcity makes relative tradeoffs matter.

cards.title: How can differences in resource abundance shape trade?
cards.answer: Countries can export goods using relatively abundant factors intensively and import goods requiring relatively scarce factors.
cards.takeaway: Trade indirectly exchanges the services of productive resources.

cards.title: How can specialization lower production costs?
cards.answer: Producing at a larger scale can spread fixed costs or improve efficiency, allowing gains beyond differences in resources or productivity.
cards.takeaway: A larger market can support more efficient production.

cards.title: Why are international borrowing and lending a form of trade?
cards.answer: They exchange resources available now for claims on resources available later.
cards.takeaway: Finance moves purchasing power through time.

cards.title: If a country gains overall from trade, must every resident gain?
cards.answer: No. Owners of resources used intensively in import-competing industries can lose even when aggregate gains are positive.
cards.takeaway: National gains and individual gains are different claims.

cards.title: What does the pattern of trade describe?
cards.answer: Who sells which goods and services to whom. Productivity, climate, and relative factor supplies help explain that pattern.
cards.takeaway: Trade composition reflects differences in production possibilities.

cards.title: How does a tariff differ from a quota?
cards.answer: A tariff taxes trade; a quota limits its quantity. Both can restrict trade but use different policy instruments.
cards.takeaway: A price wedge and a quantity ceiling are not the same mechanism.

cards.title: What is an export subsidy?
cards.answer: A payment encouraging producers to sell abroad, rather than a tax paid on imports.
cards.takeaway: Identify who receives the policy payment.

cards.title: Can trade be restricted without a tariff or quota?
cards.answer: Yes. Product rules or other regulations can exclude foreign goods while permitting domestic substitutes.
cards.takeaway: A barrier's effect can matter more than its label.

cards.title: Why consider foreign retaliation when evaluating a trade restriction?
cards.answer: Other governments may respond with their own restrictions, reducing export opportunities and changing the original policy's costs and benefits.
cards.takeaway: Policy choices can provoke responses abroad.

cards.title: Why might trade policy differ from a policy maximizing national welfare?
cards.answer: Organized groups can favor policies benefiting themselves even if the economy as a whole loses.
cards.takeaway: Concentrated benefits can outweigh diffuse costs politically.

cards.title: How can international asset trade reduce income risk?
cards.answer: Holding assets whose payoffs do not move together can reduce portfolio income variability. It does not eliminate every risk.
cards.takeaway: Different sources of income can offset one another.

cards.title: Why do exchange rates matter for trade prices?
cards.answer: They translate foreign prices into domestic currency and domestic prices into foreign currency.
cards.takeaway: The currency conversion changes affordability across borders.

cards.title: How does a floating exchange rate differ from a fixed one?
cards.answer: A floating rate can change with market conditions; a fixed regime aims to maintain a specified rate or parity through policy.
cards.takeaway: The exchange-rate regime affects policy constraints.

cards.title: Why can international policy coordination be useful?
cards.answer: One country's policies can affect other countries through trade and financial markets. Coordination can account for these spillovers.
cards.takeaway: Integrated economies are not isolated policy laboratories.

cards.title: What extra risks arise in international capital markets?
cards.answer: Exchange-rate changes can alter repayments measured in the lender's currency, and sovereign borrowers can default. Foreign-investment rules also affect transactions.
cards.takeaway: A promised foreign-currency payoff has more than one source of uncertainty.

cards.title: Why do production, expenditure, and income have equal aggregate values?
cards.answer: Spending on produced goods and services becomes income to the factors and firms producing them. They are different ways to count the same activity.
cards.takeaway: Do not add the three measures together.

cards.title: What does GNP measure?
cards.answer: The value of final goods and services produced by a nation's factors of production during a period, including their production abroad.
cards.takeaway: GNP follows the national ownership of productive factors.

cards.title: What does GDP measure?
cards.answer: The value of final goods and services produced within a country's borders during a period, regardless of factor ownership.
cards.takeaway: GDP follows the location of production.

cards.title: How do net foreign factor receipts connect GNP and GDP?
cards.answer: GNP \(=\) GDP + factor income received from abroad − factor income paid abroad.
cards.takeaway: Location and ownership differ through cross-border factor income.

cards.title: How are profits from a Spanish factory owned by British residents classified?
cards.answer: The factory's production contributes to Spain's GDP. Its British-owned factor income contributes to Britain's GNP rather than Britain's GDP.
cards.takeaway: Where production occurs is distinct from who earns its income.

cards.title: Why count final output rather than repeatedly counting intermediate inputs?
cards.answer: The final output's value already incorporates the intermediate inputs. Counting both in full would double-count production.
cards.takeaway: Value added and final expenditure avoid repeated counting.

cards.title: What are the four expenditure components in \(Y=C+I+G+CA\)?
cards.answer: Consumption, domestic investment, government purchases, and the current account balance under the chapter's simplified accounting conventions.
cards.takeaway: Identify how national output is used.

cards.title: Does buying an existing stock count as investment in national income accounting?
cards.answer: No. Here investment means additions to productive capital and inventories, not trading an existing financial claim.
cards.takeaway: Economic investment and portfolio investment use the same word differently.

cards.title: Why do firms' additions to inventories count as investment?
cards.answer: They are produced goods held for future sale or use rather than current consumption.
cards.takeaway: Unsold production is still production.

cards.title: Why subtract capital depreciation when moving from gross to net income?
cards.answer: Depreciation represents capital used up during production, so not all gross output is available without reducing the capital stock.
cards.takeaway: Gross measures include replacement of worn-out capital.

cards.title: How does a unilateral transfer differ from payment for production?
cards.answer: It transfers purchasing power without buying a good, service, or asset in return. It affects disposable resources and the current account but is not newly produced output.
cards.takeaway: A gift is a transfer of resources, not extra production.

cards.title: What is domestic absorption?
cards.answer: C+I+G: expenditure by domestic consumers, firms, and government on goods and services.
cards.takeaway: Absorption measures spending at home, not just domestic production.

cards.title: How does the current account relate to income and absorption?
cards.answer: \(CA=Y-(C+I+G)\) in the chapter's income identity. A surplus means income exceeds absorption; a deficit means absorption exceeds income.
cards.takeaway: The current account records the gap between earning and spending.

cards.title: Is the full current account always just exports minus imports of goods?
cards.answer: No. It also includes services, net primary income, and net current transfers. The chapter's simple EX−IM notation suppresses or groups these adjustments.
cards.takeaway: Do not confuse a goods trade balance with the full current account.

cards.title: How can a country finance a current account deficit?
cards.answer: By increasing liabilities to foreigners or reducing previously accumulated foreign assets, ignoring capital transfers and valuation effects.
cards.takeaway: Spending beyond income uses external financing or existing wealth.

cards.title: Does a current account deficit exactly equal the fall in measured net foreign wealth?
cards.answer: Not generally. It contributes to the change, but asset-price changes, exchange-rate revaluations, capital transfers, and other adjustments also affect the stock.
cards.takeaway: A flow does not fully explain a revalued asset stock.

cards.title: How is national saving defined in the chapter?
cards.answer: \(S=Y-C-G\): income not used for consumption or government purchases.
cards.takeaway: Saving leaves resources available for investment or net foreign lending.

cards.title: How do saving, investment, and the current account connect?
cards.answer: \(S=I+CA\), so \(CA=S-I\). Saving can fund domestic investment or a net acquisition of foreign claims.
cards.takeaway: An open economy has two destinations for saving.

cards.title: Why does national saving equal investment in a closed economy?
cards.answer: Without cross-border transactions, \(CA=0\), so the identity \(S=I+CA\) reduces to \(S=I\).
cards.takeaway: Closing the economy removes net foreign lending.

cards.title: If domestic investment exceeds national saving, what sign does CA have?
cards.answer: Negative: \(CA=S-I<0\). The investment gap is financed by net external borrowing or foreign-asset reduction.
cards.takeaway: Domestic investment need not wait for equal domestic saving.

cards.title: How do you calculate private saving from income, taxes, and consumption?
cards.answer: \(S^{p}=Y-T-C\), where T is net taxes and Y−T is disposable income.
cards.takeaway: Private saving is what remains after taxes and consumption.

cards.title: What is government saving?
cards.answer: \(S^{g}=T-G\). A budget deficit, \(G>T\), is negative government saving.
cards.takeaway: A budget deficit absorbs part of national saving.

cards.title: Why does \(S^{p}+S^{g}\) equal national saving?
cards.answer: Adding Y−T−C and T−G cancels taxes, leaving Y−C−G.
cards.takeaway: Taxes redistribute between sectors before they affect total saving through behavior.

cards.title: How can private saving be written using I, CA, and the budget deficit?
cards.answer: \(S^{p}=I+CA+(G-T)\). Rearranging gives \(CA=S^{p}-I-(G-T)\).
cards.takeaway: The budget deficit competes with investment and foreign lending for private saving.

cards.title: Must a larger government deficit cause an equal current account deterioration?
cards.answer: Only if private saving and investment stay fixed. The accounting identity alone does not say how those behaviors respond.
cards.takeaway: An identity is not a complete causal model.

cards.title: How many entries does an international transaction create in double-entry bookkeeping?
cards.answer: Two equal-value entries: one credit and one debit, possibly within the same account.
cards.takeaway: The payment side balances the resource or asset side.

cards.title: What distinguishes the current, financial, and capital accounts?
cards.answer: The current account records goods, services, income, and current transfers. The financial account records financial asset transactions. The capital account records capital transfers and certain nonproduced nonfinancial assets.
cards.takeaway: Classify the transaction before assigning its sign.

cards.title: What financial-account sign convention do these slides use?
cards.answer: Net financial inflows are positive: sales of domestic assets to foreigners minus domestic purchases of foreign assets. Under it, \(CA+KA+FA=0\).
cards.takeaway: State the sign convention before using an identity.

cards.title: Why is a resident's purchase of a foreign asset a financial-account debit in the slides?
cards.answer: It is a financial outflow: the resident gives up funds to acquire a claim on a foreign entity.
cards.takeaway: Buying a foreign claim sends financing abroad.

cards.title: Why is selling a domestic asset to a foreigner a financial-account credit?
cards.answer: It brings financing into the domestic economy and increases foreigners' claims on it.
cards.takeaway: An inflow creates a foreign-held claim, not free income.

cards.title: A U.S. resident imports a $1,000 machine and the seller keeps a U.S. bank deposit. What are the entries?
cards.answer: A $1,000 current-account debit for the goods import and a $1,000 financial-account credit for the foreign-held U.S. deposit.
cards.takeaway: The imported good and the payment claim balance.

cards.title: How is a U.S. resident's meal in France paid by credit card recorded?
cards.answer: A current-account debit for a U.S. service import and an offsetting financial credit for the payment claim, using the slides' convention.
cards.takeaway: Tourism purchases count as international trade in services.

cards.title: Can both entries for one transaction be in the financial account?
cards.answer: Yes. A U.S. resident buying a foreign share creates an asset-purchase debit; a matching increase in the foreign seller's U.S. deposit creates a credit.
cards.takeaway: No goods trade is required for a cross-border financial transaction.

cards.title: How do the slides record a U.S. bank forgiving foreign debt?
cards.answer: A capital-account debit for the transfer and a financial-account credit for reducing the bank's claim on the foreign borrower.
cards.takeaway: Forgiveness removes an asset and transfers wealth.

cards.title: If \(CA=-40\) and \(KA=5\), what is FA under the slides' net-inflow convention?
cards.takeaway: Account signs must close the same identity.

cards.title: Why can published balance-of-payments data need a statistical discrepancy?
cards.answer: Different data sources have timing, coverage, and measurement errors even though the underlying double-entry identity balances.
cards.takeaway: An accounting identity does not make measurement perfect.

cards.title: Why should all countries' current accounts sum to zero in principle?
cards.answer: Each country's payment is another country's receipt. A nonzero measured world total points to inconsistent measurement rather than trade with an outside planet.
cards.takeaway: Global credits and debits should match.

cards.title: What is official foreign exchange intervention?
cards.answer: A central bank's purchase or sale of international reserve assets in asset markets. Such transactions can also inject or withdraw domestic money.
cards.takeaway: Reserve transactions connect exchange markets with monetary conditions.

cards.title: What counts as an official international reserve asset in the slides?
cards.answer: Foreign assets held by monetary authorities, including foreign currency, government bonds, gold, and IMF-related reserve assets.
cards.takeaway: Reserves provide a buffer for external payments and instability.

cards.title: What is the official settlements balance under the slides' convention?
cards.answer: CA+KA+nonreserve financial flows+statistical discrepancy. It is the negative of the balancing net official reserve-related financial flow.
cards.takeaway: The overall accounts balance even when the official settlements balance is nonzero.

cards.title: What may a negative official settlements balance indicate?
cards.answer: Reserve depletion or increased liabilities to foreign official institutions can finance it. It does not mean double-entry bookkeeping has failed.
cards.takeaway: Official financing fills the remaining external gap.

cards.title: How is a country's net foreign wealth calculated?
cards.answer: Foreign assets owned by residents minus domestic liabilities owed to foreigners, valued at the relevant date.
cards.takeaway: Large foreign assets do not imply positive net wealth.

cards.title: How can dollar depreciation improve U.S. net foreign wealth in the slides' example?
cards.answer: Foreign-currency assets rise in dollar value while dollar-denominated liabilities do not change from that currency movement alone.
cards.takeaway: The currencies of assets and liabilities determine valuation exposure.

cards.title: How do you reconcile beginning and ending international investment positions?
cards.answer: Add financial transactions, asset-price changes, exchange-rate changes, and other volume or valuation adjustments to the opening position.
cards.takeaway: External wealth changes through both transactions and revaluation.

cards.title: Why can the international investment position contain an 'other changes' category?
cards.answer: Survey coverage, reporting-panel changes, unallocated valuation effects, and other revisions can alter measured positions without a recorded new transaction.
cards.takeaway: Measurement revisions need not represent fresh borrowing.

cards.title: What does profit shifting do to measured production in a low-tax location?
cards.answer: Booking multinational income or intellectual property there can raise measured GDP without a matching increase in local labor or living standards.
cards.takeaway: A GDP jump can reflect accounting location rather than broad prosperity.

cards.title: What is the lesson of the slides' 2015 Irish GDP jump?
cards.answer: Its unusually large rise partly reflected multinational accounting and intellectual-property relocation, so GDP growth alone was a poor guide to residents' welfare.
cards.takeaway: Treat this as a historical illustration, not a current tax-rate claim.

cards.title: What does \(E=1.20\) dollars per euro mean?
cards.answer: One euro costs 1.20 dollars. Multiplying a euro amount by E converts it to dollars; dividing a dollar amount by E converts it to euros.
cards.takeaway: Carry currency units through every calculation.

cards.title: If one euro costs $1.25, how many euros does one dollar buy?
cards.answer: \(\frac{1}{1.25}=0.80\) euros per dollar.
cards.takeaway: Reversing a quote requires taking its reciprocal.

cards.title: If E in dollars per euro rises, which currency depreciates?
cards.answer: The dollar depreciates and the euro appreciates: more dollars are required to buy one euro.
cards.takeaway: A higher quoted number does not always mean a stronger domestic currency.

cards.title: If E falls from $1.00/€ to $0.90/€, what happens to the dollar?
cards.answer: It appreciates against the euro because each dollar now buys more euros.
cards.takeaway: Interpret the quote's units before naming the movement.

cards.title: With a fixed euro sticker price, how does dollar depreciation change a U.S. import's dollar price?
cards.answer: It increases the dollar price because \(P_{\mathrm{USD}}=E\times P_{\mathrm{EUR}}\) and E rises.
cards.takeaway: Exchange-rate pass-through here assumes the foreign sticker price is unchanged.

cards.title: With a fixed dollar sticker price, how does dollar appreciation affect a U.S. export's euro price?
cards.answer: It raises the euro price: \(P_{\mathrm{EUR}}=P_{\mathrm{USD}}/E\) and dollar appreciation means E falls.
cards.takeaway: A stronger currency makes unchanged domestic-price exports costlier abroad.

cards.title: How do you express a British sweater's price in pairs of American jeans?
cards.answer: Multiply its pound price by dollars per pound, then divide by the dollar price of one pair of jeans.
cards.takeaway: Convert to a common currency before taking a relative price.

cards.title: Does depreciation mechanically guarantee an immediate export-volume increase?
cards.answer: No. It changes relative prices under the model's assumptions; quantity responses also depend on demand, contracts, and adjustment timing.
cards.takeaway: Price effects and quantity effects are not identical claims.

cards.title: Who participates in foreign exchange markets?
cards.answer: Banks, nonfinancial corporations, nonbank financial institutions, and central banks. Their motives include trade payments, investment, and official reserve management.
cards.takeaway: The market is larger than importers exchanging travel money.

cards.title: Why do banks play a central role in FX trading?
cards.answer: They buy and sell currency deposits for themselves and clients and trade extensively with other banks.
cards.takeaway: Many customer transactions are connected through the interbank market.

cards.title: How does arbitrage reduce exchange-rate differences across locations?
cards.answer: Traders buy currency where it is cheaper and sell where it is dearer, raising demand in the cheap market and supply in the expensive one.
cards.takeaway: A tradable price gap invites trades that narrow it.

cards.title: Is a tiny quoted FX price difference automatically an exploitable profit?
cards.answer: No. Fees, bid-ask spreads, timing, and execution costs can exceed the gross gap.
cards.takeaway: Compare achievable net prices, not just displayed midpoint quotes.

cards.title: How does a forward exchange contract differ from a spot transaction?
cards.answer: A spot transaction exchanges currency promptly. A forward fixes the rate now for exchange at a specified future date.
cards.takeaway: Agreement date and delivery date are different concepts.

cards.title: Must spot and forward rates be equal because they move together?
cards.answer: No. They concern different delivery dates; interest-rate differentials can create a forward premium or discount.
cards.takeaway: High correlation is not numerical equality.

cards.title: What are the two legs of the FX swap described in the slides?
cards.answer: A spot sale of one currency and a forward repurchase of it.
cards.takeaway: A swap temporarily changes the currency held.

cards.title: Why might a firm receiving dollars use an FX swap if it needs dollars again in three months?
cards.answer: It can exchange dollars into another currency now while arranging the reverse exchange for the future dollar payment.
cards.takeaway: Match temporary investment needs with known future currency needs.

cards.title: What distinguishes the futures contracts described here from customized forwards?
cards.answer: Futures use standardized contract amounts and delivery dates and can be traded in organized markets. Forwards are negotiated between parties.
cards.takeaway: Standardization supports trading and clearing.

cards.title: What is the dollar notional of ¥12,500,000 at $0.006400 per yen?
cards.answer: \(\text{JPY}12,500,000\times \text{USD}0.006400/\text{JPY}=\text{USD}80,000\).
cards.takeaway: Notional measures the position's scale, not the required collateral.

cards.title: How do you find the dollar value of a futures price tick?
cards.answer: Multiply the contract's currency amount by the price tick. Here \(\text{JPY}12,500,000\times \text{USD}0.0000005/\text{JPY}=\text{USD}6.25\).
cards.takeaway: A small quote movement is multiplied by the full contract size.

cards.title: How does initial margin differ from maintenance margin?
cards.answer: Initial margin is collateral required to open a position; maintenance margin is the minimum account equity required to keep it open under the stated rules.
cards.takeaway: Margin is not the contract's purchase price.

cards.title: Why can a modest futures price change cause a large percentage change in posted collateral?
cards.answer: Profit and loss depend on the full notional position, which can be much larger than the margin deposit.
cards.takeaway: Leverage magnifies losses as well as gains relative to collateral.

cards.title: A long yen contract rises from 0.006400 to 0.006450 $/¥. What is gross profit on ¥12.5 million?
cards.answer: The price gain is 0.000050 $/¥. Multiplying by ¥12,500,000 gives $625, or 100 ticks at $6.25.
cards.takeaway: A long currency future benefits when that currency's quoted price rises.

cards.title: With $625 gross futures profit and $2 fees at entry and exit, what is net profit?
cards.answer: \(\text{USD}625-\text{USD}2-\text{USD}2=\text{USD}621\) in the slide's example.
cards.takeaway: Round-trip costs reduce the amount actually earned.

cards.title: What separates buying an option from entering a forward obligation?
cards.answer: The option holder has a right, not an obligation, to transact under its terms. The right generally costs a premium.
cards.takeaway: Flexibility is not the same as a free guaranteed payoff.

cards.title: What is the difference between a currency call and put?
cards.answer: A call gives its holder the right to buy the specified currency; a put gives the right to sell it at the strike.
cards.takeaway: Name the underlying currency before interpreting the option.

cards.title: Can every currency option be exercised at any time before expiry?
cards.answer: No. That describes American-style exercise. European-style options are exercised only at expiry; the contract terms matter.
cards.takeaway: Do not turn one contract style into a universal definition.

cards.title: How do you calculate a one-period nominal rate of return?
cards.answer: Ending value minus initial value, divided by initial value. A $100 deposit ending at $102 returns 2%.
cards.takeaway: Return is a proportional gain, not the final account balance.

cards.title: How do you approximate a real return from a nominal return and inflation?
cards.answer: Subtract inflation: \(r\approx R-\pi\). The exact gross real return is \((1+R)/(1+\pi )\).
cards.takeaway: Purchasing-power gains can be smaller than money gains.

cards.title: Why do nominal and real returns coincide in the chapter's fixed-price short run?
cards.answer: Inflation is zero over the modeled period, so adjusting the nominal return for inflation makes no change.
cards.takeaway: The equality comes from an assumption about prices.

cards.title: Which three attributes guide asset demand?
cards.answer: Expected return, risk, and liquidity.
cards.takeaway: A higher promised interest rate is not the only consideration.

cards.title: Why does the basic currency-deposit model compare expected returns alone?
cards.answer: It treats deposits' risk and liquidity as sufficiently similar. This is a simplifying assumption, not a universal property of real deposits.
cards.takeaway: Know what the model holds constant.

cards.title: What determines a foreign deposit's return in domestic currency?
cards.answer: Its foreign-currency interest rate and the exchange-rate change between purchase and conversion back.
cards.takeaway: Currency gains can reinforce or offset interest earnings.

cards.title: How do you compute the expected dollar payoff from investing one dollar in euros?
cards.answer: Buy \(1/E\) euros, earn (1+R€)/E euros, then convert at expected future rate \(E^{e}\) to get \((1+R_{\mathrm{EUR}})E^{e}/E\) dollars.
cards.takeaway: Follow the currency conversion at both ends.

cards.title: What is the exact expected dollar return on a euro deposit in the chapter's one-period setup?
cards.answer: \(R_{\mathrm{EUR},\mathrm{USD}}=(1+R_{\mathrm{EUR}})\frac{E^e}{E}-1\), with E and \(E^{e}\) both quoted in dollars per euro.
cards.takeaway: The interest gain also experiences the currency conversion.

cards.title: What approximation does the chapter use for a euro deposit's expected dollar return?
cards.answer: \(R_{\mathrm{EUR}}+\frac{E^e-E}{E}\). It drops the product of the interest rate and the expected exchange-rate change.
cards.takeaway: The approximation works best when both rates are small.

cards.title: Why can exact and approximate foreign returns disagree?
cards.answer: The exact return includes \(R_{\mathrm{EUR}}\times [(E^{e}-E)/E]\), which the additive approximation omits.
cards.takeaway: A small omitted product is still nonzero.

cards.title: Does a 4% euro rate beat a 2% dollar rate when the euro is expected to lose 3% against the dollar?
cards.answer: No. The euro deposit's exact dollar return is \(1.04\times 0.97-1=0.88\%\), below 2%.
cards.takeaway: A currency loss can outweigh an interest advantage.

cards.title: What does \(R_{\mathrm{USD}}-R_{\mathrm{EUR}}-\frac{E^e-E}{E}\) measure?
cards.answer: The approximate expected dollar return advantage of dollar deposits over euro deposits. A positive value favors dollars under the model's assumptions.
cards.takeaway: Compare both alternatives in the same currency.

cards.title: What is the chapter's approximate uncovered interest parity condition?
cards.answer: \(R_{\mathrm{USD}}=R_{\mathrm{EUR}}+\frac{E^e-E}{E}\). Deposits offer equal expected returns measured in dollars under the model's risk and liquidity assumptions.
cards.takeaway: Uncovered means the future exchange rate is not locked in.

cards.title: Does uncovered parity eliminate exchange-rate risk?
cards.answer: No. It equates expected returns under assumptions; the realized future spot rate can differ from its expected value.
cards.takeaway: Expected equality is not a guaranteed risk-free payoff.

cards.title: If dollar deposits initially offer higher expected returns, how does E adjust in the model?
cards.answer: Demand shifts toward dollars, so E falls: the dollar appreciates. At fixed \(E^{e}\), cheaper euros now offer greater expected future appreciation until parity is restored.
cards.takeaway: Today's price adjusts to close the expected-return gap.

cards.title: At fixed \(E^{e}\) and R€, why does a higher current E lower expected euro returns?
cards.answer: It costs more dollars to acquire the same future euro payoff, reducing the percentage return.
cards.takeaway: Paying more today for the same expected payoff lowers its yield.

cards.title: At fixed \(E^{e}\) and R€, how does dollar appreciation today affect expected euro returns?
cards.answer: A lower E makes euros cheaper today and raises their expected dollar return.
cards.takeaway: Current appreciation and expected future appreciation have different effects.

cards.title: What identifies equilibrium in the chapter's FX return diagram?
cards.answer: The intersection of the vertical dollar-return line and the downward-sloping expected euro-return curve, with E on the vertical axis.
cards.takeaway: Compare expected returns at each possible spot rate.

cards.title: At fixed foreign interest and \(E^{e}\), what does a higher dollar interest rate do to E?
cards.answer: It lowers E, so the dollar appreciates.
cards.takeaway: The condition on expected values is essential.

cards.title: At fixed dollar interest and \(E^{e}\), what does a higher euro interest rate do to E?
cards.answer: It raises E, so the dollar depreciates and the euro appreciates.
cards.takeaway: A higher foreign return increases demand for foreign deposits.

cards.title: Why can expected future euro appreciation strengthen the euro immediately?
cards.answer: It raises expected dollar returns on euro assets, increasing demand for euros now. E rises to restore parity.
cards.takeaway: Asset prices respond to expected future payoffs today.

cards.title: How do you solve approximate UIP for today's E?
cards.answer: \(E=\frac{E^e}{1+R_{\mathrm{USD}}-R_{\mathrm{EUR}}}\), assuming the denominator is positive.
cards.takeaway: A higher expected future quote raises today's equilibrium quote.

cards.title: Why might someone borrow in one currency and invest in another with a higher interest rate?
cards.answer: They seek the interest-rate difference. This carry trade usually leaves exchange-rate risk: depreciation of the investment currency can erase the interest gain.
cards.takeaway: The interest spread is only one part of the total return.
cards.source: Chapter 3 · Carry trade and covered parity

cards.title: Why is a carry trade not a guaranteed profit?
cards.answer: The high-interest currency may depreciate sharply, and financing, liquidity, and risk conditions can change.
cards.takeaway: Small regular gains can coexist with rare large losses.
cards.source: Chapter 3 · Carry trade and covered parity

cards.title: What changes when a foreign deposit is covered with a forward contract?
cards.answer: The investor fixes the future conversion rate F today, replacing uncertain future spot conversion with contracted conversion.
cards.takeaway: Covering removes that exchange-rate uncertainty, subject to contract performance.
cards.source: Chapter 3 · Carry trade and covered parity

cards.title: What is exact covered interest parity for one matching investment period?
cards.answer: \(1+R_{\mathrm{USD}}=(1+R_{\mathrm{EUR}})F/E\), with E and F in dollars per euro.
cards.takeaway: Compare two locked-in payoffs for the same initial dollar.
cards.source: Chapter 3 · Carry trade and covered parity

cards.title: How is the euro's forward premium against the dollar calculated?
cards.answer: It is (F−E)/E for matching spot and forward quotes in dollars per euro, over the contract period.
cards.takeaway: The premium compares forward with spot, not with an expected spot rate.
cards.source: Chapter 3 · Carry trade and covered parity

cards.title: What is the chapter's approximate covered parity relation?
cards.answer: \(R_{\mathrm{USD}}\approx R_{\mathrm{EUR}}+\frac{F-E}{E}\). It neglects the interest-times-premium cross-term.
cards.takeaway: Label the approximation when doing numerical exercises.
cards.source: Chapter 3 · Carry trade and covered parity

cards.title: How do you solve exact covered parity for the forward rate?
cards.answer: \(F=E\frac{1+R_{\mathrm{USD}}}{1+R_{\mathrm{EUR}}}\). Interest rates must cover the same maturity as the forward.
cards.takeaway: A quoted annual rate cannot be mixed blindly with a shorter contract.
cards.source: Chapter 3 · Carry trade and covered parity

cards.title: If a covered euro investment pays more dollars than dollar borrowing costs, what is the idealized arbitrage direction?
cards.answer: Borrow dollars, buy euros spot, invest in euros, and sell the euro payoff forward. At maturity, use the locked-in dollars to repay the loan.
cards.takeaway: The forward fixes the currency leg of the round trip.
cards.source: Chapter 3 · Carry trade and covered parity

cards.title: Why can measured covered-parity deviations persist rather than vanish immediately?
cards.answer: Funding costs, balance-sheet constraints, credit risk, and market frictions can prevent cheap unlimited execution. The slides document deviations around and after the financial crisis.
cards.takeaway: A textbook arbitrage assumes access and costs that real institutions may not have.
cards.source: Chapter 3 · Carry trade and covered parity

cards.title: When does the forward rate equal the expected future spot rate in these models?
cards.answer: When both covered and uncovered parity hold for comparable deposits and maturities under the stated assumptions. Covered parity alone does not imply \(F=E^{e}\).
cards.takeaway: A forward price is not automatically a forecast.
cards.source: Chapter 3 · Carry trade and covered parity

cards.title: What makes an asset money in the chapter's model?
cards.answer: It is widely accepted as a means of payment. Currency and spendable checking balances are central examples.
cards.takeaway: Money's defining service is payment convenience.

cards.title: Why can different definitions of money give different totals?
cards.answer: Narrow definitions include the most immediately spendable assets; broader definitions include additional liquid substitutes.
cards.takeaway: Liquidity is a spectrum, so the boundary is partly conventional.

cards.title: What makes an asset liquid?
cards.answer: It can be used for payment or converted into payment funds quickly with little cost.
cards.takeaway: Liquidity concerns ease of use, not simply a high resale price.

cards.title: Why hold money if other assets pay more interest?
cards.answer: Money provides payment convenience and avoids the costs of repeatedly converting other assets into spendable funds.
cards.takeaway: Liquidity services compensate for forgone interest.

cards.title: How does the central bank influence money supply in the chapter?
cards.answer: It directly controls currency issuance and influences deposit creation and other monetary assets through the banking system.
cards.takeaway: Control is not identical for every component of broad money.

cards.title: Why can holding money be risky even if its nominal value is fixed?
cards.answer: Unexpected inflation reduces the goods and services that the same nominal balance can buy.
cards.takeaway: Nominal safety does not guarantee purchasing-power safety.

cards.title: What is the opportunity cost of holding non-interest-bearing money?
cards.answer: The interest or return forgone on alternative assets.
cards.takeaway: As alternative yields rise, idle balances become more expensive to hold.

cards.title: At fixed income and prices, how does a higher interest rate affect money demand?
cards.answer: It lowers money demand by increasing the opportunity cost of holding monetary assets.
cards.takeaway: The real money-demand curve slopes down in the interest rate.

cards.title: At fixed real income and interest, how does a doubling of P affect nominal money demand?
cards.answer: It doubles nominal money demand while real money demand stays unchanged.
cards.takeaway: The same real transactions need twice as many currency units.

cards.title: Why does higher real income increase desired money holdings?
cards.answer: Higher production and expenditure create more transactions requiring liquidity.
cards.takeaway: More economic activity raises transactions demand.

cards.title: What is the aggregate nominal money-demand equation?
cards.answer: \(M^d=P L(R,Y)\), where real money demand L falls with R and rises with Y.
cards.takeaway: Separate the price scale from desired purchasing power.

cards.title: If the money stock stays fixed but prices double, what happens to purchasing power?
cards.answer: Real money balances \(M/P\) halve. Dividing nominal money by the price level shows how much goods and services that money can buy.
cards.takeaway: Dividing by the price level converts currency units into real units.

cards.title: How does an income increase differ from an interest-rate decrease in the money-demand graph?
cards.answer: Higher income shifts the entire L(R,Y) curve outward; a lower interest rate moves along a given curve.
cards.takeaway: Distinguish a changed determinant from movement along the relationship.

cards.title: What equation determines the equilibrium interest rate at fixed P and Y?
cards.answer: \(M^{s}/P=L(R,Y)\). The interest rate adjusts until real money demand equals real supply.
cards.takeaway: Equilibrium removes excess demand or supply of money.

cards.title: Why is the real money-supply line vertical in the chapter's graph?
cards.answer: Given the nominal stock and price level, \(M^{s}/P\) does not depend on the interest rate in this simplified model.
cards.takeaway: Verticality is a model assumption about supply.

cards.title: What happens when people hold more money than they want at the current interest rate?
cards.answer: They try to buy interest-bearing assets. Bond prices rise and yields fall until holding the supplied money becomes desirable.
cards.takeaway: Portfolio rebalancing changes prices; it does not let everyone eliminate money at once.

cards.title: What happens when people want more money than they currently hold?
cards.answer: They sell nonmonetary assets to obtain liquidity, putting downward pressure on bond prices and upward pressure on interest rates.
cards.takeaway: An excess demand for money is an excess supply of other assets.

cards.title: At fixed P and Y, what does a larger money supply do to the interest rate?
cards.answer: It lowers the equilibrium interest rate, increasing demand for the additional real balances.
cards.takeaway: State the fixed-price assumption before applying this result.

cards.title: At fixed real money supply, does higher real income raise or lower the equilibrium interest rate?
cards.answer: It raises it. Money demand shifts outward, so the rate must rise to offset that increase. Figure 4.5 shows this despite a mistaken caption saying 'reduces'.
cards.takeaway: Use the equilibrium condition and graph to resolve the caption error.

cards.title: At fixed nominal money supply and income, what does a higher price level do to the interest rate?
cards.answer: It reduces real money supply \(M^{s}/P\) and raises the equilibrium interest rate.
cards.takeaway: A price increase can tighten real liquidity without changing nominal money.

cards.topic: Money and FX in the short run
cards.title: With sticky prices, fixed output, and fixed exchange-rate expected values, how does a domestic monetary expansion affect the currency?
cards.answer: It increases real balances, lowers domestic interest, and depreciates the domestic currency.
cards.takeaway: Money-market changes feed into expected asset returns.
cards.source: Chapter 4 · Money and FX in the short run

cards.topic: Money and FX in the short run
cards.title: Under the same short-run assumptions, what does a domestic monetary contraction do?
cards.answer: It reduces real balances, raises domestic interest, and appreciates the domestic currency.
cards.takeaway: Reverse the whole causal chain, not only its final step.
cards.source: Chapter 4 · Money and FX in the short run

cards.topic: Money and FX in the short run
cards.title: What does a temporary European money-supply increase do to the dollar/euro quote in the model?
cards.answer: It lowers euro interest and reduces E in dollars per euro: the euro depreciates and the dollar appreciates.
cards.takeaway: The foreign monetary expansion changes the foreign-return curve.
cards.source: Chapter 4 · Money and FX in the short run

cards.topic: Money and FX in the short run
cards.title: Does the temporary European monetary expansion shift the U.S. money-market equilibrium in this model?
cards.answer: No. U.S. money supply, prices, and income are held fixed, so the U.S. interest rate is unchanged.
cards.takeaway: The FX market can move while the domestic money market stays put.
cards.source: Chapter 4 · Money and FX in the short run

cards.topic: Money and FX in the short run
cards.title: Which two conditions must hold in the combined money/FX diagram?
cards.answer: Domestic real money supply equals real money demand, and currency deposits offer equal expected returns under UIP.
cards.takeaway: One rate links the two equilibrium conditions.
cards.source: Chapter 4 · Money and FX in the short run

cards.title: What separates the short run from the long run here?
cards.answer: In the short run, some prices and wages are sticky. In the long run, they have adjusted and real output reflects productive capacity.
cards.takeaway: The distinction is about adjustment, not a fixed calendar duration.

cards.title: What determines long-run real output in this framework?
cards.answer: Labor, capital, technology, and other productive resources rather than the nominal quantity of money.
cards.takeaway: Printing currency does not itself create productive capacity.

cards.title: What is long-run neutrality of a one-time money-level change?
cards.answer: A proportional money increase eventually raises the price level proportionally without changing real output or long-run real interest in the model.
cards.takeaway: Distinguish nominal scaling from real resource changes.

cards.title: How can money-market equilibrium determine the long-run price level?
cards.answer: \(P=M^{s}/L(R,Y)\). With real money demand unchanged, prices scale with nominal money supply.
cards.takeaway: Prices adjust to restore desired real balances.

cards.title: How does the chapter relate inflation to money and real money-demand growth?
cards.answer: Approximately, inflation equals nominal money growth minus real money-demand growth.
cards.takeaway: Some new money accommodates growing demand for liquidity rather than higher prices.

cards.title: What pattern do the slides' historical money-growth and inflation data illustrate?
cards.answer: Higher sustained money growth tends to accompany higher inflation, though the relationship is not exact in every observation.
cards.takeaway: Long-run association does not imply identical short-run timing.

cards.title: Why can hyperinflation undermine money's usefulness?
cards.answer: Rapid loss of purchasing power makes holding the currency costly and can lead people to avoid using it.
cards.takeaway: An asset can lose its payment role when its real value collapses.

cards.title: How can a money expansion eventually put upward pressure on wages and output prices?
cards.answer: Higher spending increases demand for goods and labor. Producers may raise prices or pay higher wages as resources become harder to obtain.
cards.takeaway: Sticky prices can respond gradually to demand and cost pressure.

cards.title: How can expected inflation influence wages and prices before it is fully realized?
cards.answer: Workers seek compensation for expected purchasing-power loss, and firms expecting higher output prices may agree to higher wages.
cards.takeaway: Expectations can affect current price-setting decisions.

cards.title: What does much greater exchange-rate volatility than price-level-ratio volatility suggest?
cards.answer: Financial prices adjust faster than aggregate goods prices, consistent with short-run price stickiness.
cards.takeaway: Asset markets can jump while goods prices move slowly.

cards.title: What is the long-run currency effect of a permanent money-level increase, other things equal?
cards.answer: A proportional depreciation in the quoted domestic price of foreign currency, alongside a proportional domestic price-level rise.
cards.takeaway: The eventual nominal change matches the money-level change in the model.

cards.title: Why can a permanent money expansion depreciate the currency more initially than a temporary one?
cards.answer: Besides lowering current interest, it raises the expected future domestic-currency price of foreign currency.
cards.takeaway: Permanent policy changes both today's return and tomorrow's expected exchange rate.

cards.title: What does exchange-rate overshooting mean?
cards.answer: The immediate exchange-rate response exceeds its eventual long-run response, followed by partial reversal.
cards.takeaway: Overshooting is about the path, not just a large movement.

cards.title: Why does a temporarily low domestic interest rate require expected currency appreciation under UIP?
cards.answer: The lower interest return must be offset by an expected currency gain. After an expansion, E jumps above its future level so it can be expected to fall.
cards.takeaway: The anticipated reversal compensates for the interest disadvantage.

cards.title: After permanent monetary expansion, how do P, R, and E evolve toward the new long run?
cards.answer: P rises gradually, real balances decline from their initial jump, R recovers, and E falls from its overshoot while remaining above its original level.
cards.takeaway: The currency partially recovers but does not undo the permanent depreciation.

cards.title: Would immediate proportional price adjustment create the same liquidity-driven overshoot?
cards.answer: No. Real money balances would not temporarily rise, so the temporary interest-rate fall driving that overshoot would disappear.
cards.takeaway: Different adjustment speeds are central to overshooting.

cards.title: What is the mirror-image overshooting path after a permanent money contraction?
cards.answer: The currency initially appreciates beyond its long-run appreciation, then partly depreciates as prices fall and interest returns toward its long-run level.
cards.takeaway: The sign reverses, but the adjustment logic is the same.

cards.title: Can inflation news coincide with currency appreciation rather than depreciation?
cards.answer: Yes, if it raises expected policy interest rates enough relative to other changes. This conditional news response differs from a permanent inflation-driven depreciation model.
cards.takeaway: Identify what the news changes, especially expected policy and returns.

cards.title: What are the long-run exchange-rate models intended to explain?
cards.answer: How exchange rates tend to relate to economic fundamentals after prices adjust, and how investors may form future-rate expected values. They are not exact daily forecasting machines.
cards.takeaway: A long-run benchmark is not a promise about tomorrow's quote.

cards.title: What does the law of one price say?
cards.answer: Identical goods should have equal common-currency prices across competitive markets when transport costs and trade barriers are negligible.
cards.takeaway: Arbitrage links comparable goods when they can move freely.

cards.title: How do you express the law of one price for a good sold in the U.S. and Canada?
cards.answer: \(P_{\mathrm{US}}=E_{\mathrm{USD}/\mathrm{CAD}}P_{\mathrm{Canada}}\) for the same good.
cards.takeaway: The exchange-rate units must cancel the foreign currency.

cards.title: How does PPP extend the law of one price?
cards.answer: It compares the common-currency cost of equivalent baskets rather than one identical good.
cards.takeaway: Basket comparability is an additional requirement.

cards.title: What exchange rate does absolute PPP imply?
cards.answer: \(E=\frac{P}{P^*}\), where E is domestic currency per foreign currency and P and P* price equivalent baskets.
cards.takeaway: A foreign currency's price reflects the relative cost of the basket.

cards.title: If a basket costs US$200 and C$400, what is the PPP quote in U.S. dollars per Canadian dollar?
cards.answer: \(\frac{200}{400}=US\text{USD}0.50\) per C$1. The reciprocal is C$2 per US$1.
cards.takeaway: A correct ratio can still be mislabeled if quote units are omitted.

cards.title: What does relative PPP predict about exchange-rate changes?
cards.answer: Domestic-currency depreciation approximately equals domestic inflation minus foreign inflation: \(\Delta E/E\approx \pi -\pi *\).
cards.takeaway: Higher relative inflation erodes the domestic currency's purchasing power.

cards.title: What is the exact gross exchange-rate change under relative PPP?
cards.answer: \(\frac{E_1}{E_0}=\frac{1+\pi}{1+\pi^*}\). The inflation-difference formula is a small-rate approximation.
cards.takeaway: Ratios of gross growth factors preserve compounding.

cards.title: Can relative PPP hold even if absolute PPP fails?
cards.answer: Yes. A persistent level wedge can leave E proportional to \(P/P^{*}\) without making the proportionality constant one.
cards.takeaway: Stable deviations in levels can cancel when comparing growth rates.

cards.title: If both countries have equal inflation, what does relative PPP predict for E?
cards.answer: No systematic change in E from the inflation differential alone.
cards.takeaway: Compare inflation across countries, not only at home.

cards.title: What two conditions build the monetary approach to exchange rates?
cards.answer: Money-market equilibrium in each country and absolute PPP linking their price levels.
cards.takeaway: Money determines prices; PPP translates relative prices into E.

cards.title: How can E be written using money supplies and real money demands under absolute PPP?
cards.answer: \(E=\frac{M}{M^*}\frac{L(R^*,Y^*)}{L(R,Y)}\). It follows by substituting \(P=M/L\) and \(P^{*}=M^{*}/L^{*}\) into \(E=\frac{P}{P^*}\).
cards.takeaway: Relative supply and relative demand for money both matter.

cards.title: With real money demand and foreign conditions fixed, what does a 10% permanent domestic money increase do to E in the monetary model?
cards.answer: It raises P and E by 10%, a domestic depreciation.
cards.takeaway: This is a money-level experiment, not a change in its continuing growth rate.

cards.title: Under the same assumptions, how does higher foreign money supply affect E?
cards.answer: It raises the foreign price level and lowers domestic currency per foreign currency: domestic appreciation.
cards.takeaway: The foreign price level is in the denominator.

cards.title: Why can higher nominal domestic interest accompany depreciation in the monetary approach?
cards.answer: Higher nominal interest lowers desired real money balances. At fixed M, a higher P restores money-market equilibrium, and PPP implies a higher E.
cards.takeaway: This flexible-price mechanism differs from the fixed-expected values short-run asset experiment.

cards.title: At fixed M, interest, and foreign conditions, how does higher domestic output affect E under the monetary approach?
cards.answer: It raises real money demand, lowers P, and lowers E: domestic appreciation.
cards.takeaway: A stronger demand for domestic purchasing power can support the currency.

cards.title: How does a one-time money-level increase differ from a permanently higher money-growth rate?
cards.answer: The first changes the eventual price level; the second changes continuing inflation, holding real money-demand growth fixed.
cards.takeaway: A step change and a steeper trend are different shocks.

cards.title: Which assumptions connect nominal interest differentials to expected inflation differentials?
cards.answer: Uncovered interest parity plus expected relative PPP give \(R-R^{*}\approx \pi ^{e}-\pi ^{*e}\).
cards.takeaway: The Fisher differential needs an exchange-rate expected value link.

cards.title: What does the Fisher effect predict when expected inflation rises and the real interest rate stays fixed?
cards.answer: Nominal interest rises by approximately the same amount.
cards.takeaway: Lenders require compensation for expected loss of purchasing power.

cards.title: Does a high nominal interest rate always signal a strong currency?
cards.answer: No. It can reflect expected inflation and depreciation rather than an attractive real return.
cards.takeaway: Ask why the interest rate is high.

cards.title: In the flexible-price model, what happens to nominal interest after an unanticipated permanent rise in money growth?
cards.answer: Expected inflation and nominal interest rise immediately through the Fisher effect, holding the real rate fixed.
cards.takeaway: Persistent expected inflation changes nominal yields.

cards.title: Why can P jump immediately when money-growth policy changes even though M has not yet jumped?
cards.answer: The higher nominal interest rate reduces L(R,Y). At fixed current M, \(P=M/L\) must rise to clear the money market.
cards.takeaway: A change in money demand can move prices without an immediate money-stock jump.

cards.title: After the flexible-price model's initial P and E jumps, how do their paths change?
cards.answer: Prices rise at the new higher inflation rate, and the domestic currency depreciates faster under relative PPP.
cards.takeaway: An initial level adjustment is followed by a new trend.

cards.title: Why does the flexible-price monetary approach not produce the same sticky-price overshoot?
cards.answer: Prices adjust immediately with expected values, preventing the temporary excess real balances and interest-rate fall of the sticky-price mechanism.
cards.takeaway: Speed of price adjustment changes the exchange-rate path.

cards.title: Why is 'higher interest appreciates the currency' compatible with inflation-driven depreciation and higher interest?
cards.answer: The first holds future exchange-rate expected values fixed in a short-run experiment. The second changes expected inflation and future exchange rates in a long-run experiment.
cards.takeaway: Comparative statics cannot be combined while silently changing what is held fixed.

cards.title: How well do the slides say PPP predicts actual exchange rates?
cards.answer: Absolute PPP has weak empirical support. Relative PPP is often more plausible but still performs poorly as a precise exchange-rate predictor.
cards.takeaway: A useful benchmark can have large and persistent deviations.

cards.title: Why can transport costs allow the same good to have different prices across countries?
cards.answer: A price gap smaller than shipping and trade costs need not offer profitable arbitrage.
cards.takeaway: Arbitrage constrains gaps only after its costs are paid.

cards.title: Why do nontradable services weaken PPP?
cards.answer: Services such as local haircuts cannot readily be shipped from the cheaper market to the expensive one.
cards.takeaway: Local markets need not share a single world price.

cards.title: What is pricing to market?
cards.answer: Charging different prices in different markets according to local demand and competition rather than applying one uniform converted price.
cards.takeaway: Market segmentation can let firms sustain price differences.

cards.title: Why can national price-index differences make PPP tests difficult?
cards.answer: Countries' representative baskets, weights, and measurement methods differ, so their indexes may not compare identical purchases.
cards.takeaway: Comparing unlike baskets is not a clean one-price test.

cards.title: Which broad cross-country price pattern do the slides highlight?
cards.answer: Richer countries tend to have higher common-currency price levels, especially for nontradables.
cards.takeaway: A market exchange rate does not equalize all local living costs.

cards.title: How does the Balassa–Samuelson mechanism connect tradable productivity to nontradable prices?
cards.answer: High tradable-sector productivity supports high wages. Labor-market competition transmits those wages to nontradables, raising their costs and prices even without equally high nontradable productivity.
cards.takeaway: Tradable productivity can make local services expensive.

cards.title: Why can low tradable productivity help explain cheaper services in poorer countries?
cards.answer: With similar world tradable prices, lower productivity supports lower wages, which lower the cost of producing local services.
cards.takeaway: Cheap services need not imply cheap identical traded goods.

cards.title: How does the alternative factor-endowment explanation differ from Balassa–Samuelson?
cards.answer: It emphasizes higher capital per worker raising wages in rich countries, combined with labor-intensive nontradables, rather than primarily sectoral productivity differences.
cards.takeaway: Different mechanisms can produce similar aggregate price patterns.

cards.title: What is \(q=\frac{EP^*}{P}\) when E is domestic currency per foreign currency?
cards.answer: The domestic-currency cost of a foreign basket divided by the cost of a domestic basket: a relative goods price.
cards.takeaway: The real exchange rate compares purchasing power over goods, not currency units alone.

cards.title: If \(E=\text{USD}1.20/\text{EUR}\), \(P^{*}=\text{EUR}100\), and \(P=\text{USD}120\), what is q?
cards.answer: \(q=1.20\times \frac{100}{120}=1\). One foreign basket costs the same as one domestic basket.
cards.takeaway: All three inputs are needed to measure real purchasing power.

cards.title: Under \(q=\frac{EP^*}{P}\), what does a rise in q mean?
cards.answer: Domestic real depreciation: foreign goods become more expensive relative to domestic goods.
cards.takeaway: State the convention because reciprocal definitions reverse the direction.

cards.title: Under \(q=\frac{EP^*}{P}\), what does a fall in q mean?
cards.answer: Domestic real appreciation: domestic goods become more expensive relative to foreign goods.
cards.takeaway: Real appreciation concerns relative goods prices.

cards.title: How do you recover the nominal exchange rate from q and price levels?
cards.answer: \(E=q\frac{P}{P^*}\). Nominal movements can reflect either relative price levels or real relative-price changes.
cards.takeaway: PPP is the special case with a fixed appropriate q.

cards.title: Must nominal depreciation imply real depreciation?
cards.answer: No. If domestic prices rise proportionally with E while foreign prices stay fixed, \(q=\frac{EP^*}{P}\) is unchanged.
cards.takeaway: Inflation can offset a nominal exchange-rate movement.

cards.title: How does higher relative world demand for domestic goods affect q in the long run?
cards.answer: It lowers q, a domestic real appreciation, as domestic goods become relatively more expensive.
cards.takeaway: Higher demand raises the relative value of the desired output.

cards.title: In the chapter's aggregate relative-supply model, how does more domestic output affect q?
cards.answer: It raises q, a real depreciation, to encourage the world to absorb the increased relative supply.
cards.takeaway: More output must be sold at a sufficiently attractive relative price.

cards.title: Why does the relative-demand curve rise with q in Figure 5.4?
cards.answer: A higher q makes domestic goods cheaper relative to foreign goods, increasing relative demand for domestic output.
cards.takeaway: Here the vertical-axis variable is the foreign-to-domestic goods price.

cards.title: Why is long-run relative supply drawn vertically in Figure 5.4?
cards.answer: Full-employment relative output is taken as given by productive capacity in this simplified diagram.
cards.takeaway: The graph isolates a relative-price adjustment to given output.

cards.title: When only monetary factors change in the long-run PPP benchmark, what happens to q?
cards.answer: It remains unchanged; P and E adjust consistently with the monetary change.
cards.takeaway: Nominal scaling alone need not change relative goods prices.

cards.title: Holding price levels fixed, how does higher demand for domestic goods affect nominal E?
cards.answer: Real appreciation lowers q, so \(E=q\frac{P}{P^*}\) falls: nominal domestic appreciation.
cards.takeaway: A real demand shift can move the currency without a money-supply change.

cards.title: Why is higher domestic output's effect on nominal E ambiguous in the general model?
cards.answer: More output raises q through real depreciation but increases money demand and lowers P. Since \(E=q\frac{P}{P^*}\), those effects oppose each other.
cards.takeaway: A clear real effect need not determine the nominal effect.

cards.title: Why needn't aggregate-output real depreciation contradict Balassa–Samuelson appreciation?
cards.answer: The aggregate relative-supply exercise and the sector-specific tradable-productivity mechanism change different things. Sectoral composition and nontradable wages matter in the latter.
cards.takeaway: Specify which productivity experiment is being analyzed.

cards.title: What adds to the inflation differential in the general nominal interest differential?
cards.answer: Expected real depreciation: R−R*≈expected \(\Delta q/q+\pi ^{e}-\pi ^{*e}\), combining UIP with \(q=\frac{EP^*}{P}\).
cards.takeaway: Expected goods-price changes matter when relative PPP does not hold.

cards.title: What is the approximate expected real interest rate?
cards.answer: \(r^{e}\approx R-\pi ^{e}\). It measures the expected purchasing-power return rather than the currency-unit return.
cards.takeaway: Expected inflation, not already realized inflation, enters an ex ante calculation.

cards.title: What does real interest parity predict under the chapter's assumptions?
cards.answer: \(r^e-r^{*e}\approx\mathbb{E}[\Delta q/q]\). The real return gap matches expected domestic real depreciation.
cards.takeaway: Equal expected nominal-currency returns need not mean equal goods-basket returns.

cards.title: When does real interest parity imply equal real interest rates across countries?
cards.answer: When the real exchange rate is expected to stay constant, including the relative-PPP benchmark.
cards.takeaway: Equal real rates require more than capital-market integration alone.

cards.title: If expected real domestic depreciation is 2% and the foreign real rate is 1%, what is the domestic real rate under approximate real parity?
cards.answer: 3%: the domestic real rate exceeds the foreign rate by the expected 2% real depreciation.
cards.takeaway: Keep the sign tied to \(q=\frac{EP^*}{P}\).

cards.title: Why might traders exchange two currencies through dollars instead of trading the pair directly?
cards.answer: Dollar markets can be deeper and easier to trade. The dollar acts as an intermediary, called a vehicle currency, even when neither trader is American.
cards.takeaway: A widely used trading network can reduce the need for every possible direct currency pair.

cards.title: Why is an ordinary bond not classified like a forward, future, option, or swap?
cards.answer: An ordinary bond is a debt claim. The other contracts derive payoffs from specified underlying prices, rates, or exchanges.
cards.takeaway: Do not classify every financial asset as a derivative.

cards.title: How can electronic payment innovations change money demand at a given income and interest rate?
cards.answer: They can change how much spendable balance is needed for transactions, shifting the money-demand relationship rather than merely moving along it.
cards.takeaway: Payment technology can alter desired liquidity.

cards.title: What dollar amount buys a £50 sweater at $1.25 per pound?
cards.answer: $62.50: \(50\times 1.25\). The pound units cancel, leaving dollars.
cards.takeaway: Use multiplication when the quote is domestic currency per foreign currency.

cards.title: If identical jeans cost $50 and £100, what dollar-per-pound rate equalizes their prices?
cards.answer: $0.50 per pound, assuming the prices are linked by the law of one price. Prices alone do not reveal the actual market exchange rate without that assumption.
cards.takeaway: An implied parity rate is not automatically an observed market quote.

cards.title: With \(E=\text{USD}1.10/\text{EUR}\), \(E^{e}=\text{USD}1.165/\text{EUR}\), and \(R_{\mathrm{EUR}}=5\%\), why is the homework return about 11%?

cards.takeaway: Rounded choices can hide a meaningful distinction between formulas.

cards.title: At \(E=\text{USD}1.00/\text{EUR}\), \(R_{\mathrm{USD}}=10\%\), and \(R_{\mathrm{EUR}}=5\%\), what one-year forward quote satisfies parity?

cards.takeaway: Do not mix the approximate premium with an exact no-arbitrage claim.
