cards.title: A can make 10 shirts or 5 shoes; B can make 6 shirts or 2 shoes. Who has comparative advantage in shoes?
cards.answer: A: one shoe costs A two shirts but costs B three shirts. A has lower opportunity cost in shoes even though it is also absolutely more productive in shirts.
cards.takeaway: Relative opportunity cost identifies the specialization margin.
cards.source: Chapter 1 · Gains from trade · authored companion

cards.title: What is wrong with saying aggregate gains from trade prove no compensation is needed?
cards.answer: Aggregate gains do not guarantee every group gains. Import-competing workers or factor owners may lose; whether and how to compensate is a separate policy question.
cards.takeaway: An aggregate improvement can coexist with concentrated losses.
cards.source: Chapter 1 · Gains from trade · authored companion

items.label: Claim
items.value: The country gains, so nobody loses.

cards.title: If GDP is 500, foreign factor receipts are 40, and factor payments abroad are 25, what is GNP?
cards.answer: 515: 500+40−25. Net foreign factor income is 15.
cards.takeaway: Use net receipts rather than adding all receipts alone.
cards.source: Chapter 2 · National income accounting · authored companion

cards.title: What finishes the accounting chain if \(Y=200\), \(C=120\), \(G=30\), and \(I=65\)?
cards.answer: Saving is \(200-120-30=50\). \(CA=50-65=-15\), a current account deficit.
cards.takeaway: Subtract domestic investment from saving after computing saving.
cards.source: Chapter 2 · Saving and investment · authored companion

cards.title: If CA+KA+nonreserve FA+discrepancy=−12, what official flow balances the accounts?
cards.answer: A +12 net official financing credit under the slides’ convention. This can reflect reserve sales or additional foreign official claims.
cards.takeaway: A negative settlements balance needs positive official financing.
cards.source: Chapter 2 · Reserves and external wealth · authored companion

cards.title: With €100 of assets and $80 of liabilities, what happens to net dollar wealth when E rises from 1 to 1.2 $/€?
cards.answer: It rises from $20 to $40: assets rise from $100 to $120 while liabilities stay $80, assuming nothing else changes.
cards.takeaway: Currency revaluation can change wealth without any new saving.
cards.source: Chapter 2 · Reserves and external wealth · authored companion

cards.title: An opening net position is −100; transactions add −10, price gains add 8, and currency gains add 7. What is the ending position?
cards.answer: −95: −100−10+8+7. The position improves despite negative net transactions.
cards.takeaway: Valuation gains can outweigh a negative transaction flow.
cards.source: Chapter 2 · Reserves and external wealth · authored companion

cards.title: What is wrong with saying a rise from $1.00/€ to $1.20/€ means dollar appreciation?
cards.answer: The dollar depreciates: it buys fewer euros. The euro’s dollar price rises 20%, while the dollar’s euro value falls from 1 to \(\frac{1}{1.2}\approx 0.8333\), about 16.67%.
cards.takeaway: Reciprocal quotes have opposite signs and different percentage magnitudes.

items.label: Claim
items.value: More dollars per euro means a stronger dollar.

cards.title: If euros cost $1.10 in one market and $1.12 in another, what is gross profit on an immediate €1,000 round trip?
cards.answer: Buy at $1.10 and sell at $1.12 for a gross $20 profit before fees, spreads, and execution risk.
cards.takeaway: A price gap only becomes profit if both legs are executable.
cards.source: Chapter 3 · Foreign exchange markets · authored companion

cards.title: If \(E^{e}=\text{USD}1.20/\text{EUR}\), \(R_{\mathrm{USD}}=10\%\), and \(R_{\mathrm{EUR}}=5\%\), what is today’s approximate UIP equilibrium E?
cards.answer: \(E=1.20/(1+0.10-0.05)\approx \text{USD}1.14286/\text{EUR}\). This leaves expected dollar depreciation of 5%, offsetting the euro interest disadvantage.
cards.takeaway: Solve for today’s price rather than plugging the future rate in as today’s rate.
cards.source: Chapter 3 · Interest parity and expectations · authored companion

cards.title: Does \(F=\text{USD}1.113/\text{EUR}\), \(E=\text{USD}1.05/\text{EUR}\), \(R_{\mathrm{EUR}}=4\%\), and \(R_{\mathrm{USD}}=10\%\) satisfy exact CIP?
cards.answer: No. The covered euro return is \(1.04\times \frac{1.113}{1.05}-1=10.24\%\), above 10%. Exact parity requires \(F=1.05\times \frac{1.10}{1.04}\approx \text{USD}1.11058/\text{EUR}\). The additive approximation hides the gap.
cards.takeaway: An approximate equality is not exact no-arbitrage.
cards.source: Chapter 3 · Covered parity practice · authored companion

cards.title: If nominal balances rise from 100 to 120 while P rises from 2 to 3, did real balances rise?
cards.answer: No. They fell from \(\frac{100}{2}=50\) to \(\frac{120}{3}=40\), a 20% decrease.
cards.takeaway: More currency units can still buy fewer goods.

cards.topic: Money and FX in the short run
cards.title: What completes the temporary U.S. expansion chain with fixed prices, output, and expected values?
cards.answer: Higher U.S. real money supply lowers dollar interest; dollar deposits become less attractive, so E in dollars per euro rises and the dollar depreciates.
cards.takeaway: Carry the money-market result into the FX market.
cards.source: Chapter 4 · Money and FX in the short run · authored companion

cards.title: If nominal money grows 8% and real money demand grows 3%, what inflation rate does the growth approximation predict?
cards.answer: About 5%. The exact gross-rate calculation is \(\frac{1.08}{1.03}-1\approx 4.85\%\).
cards.takeaway: State when you use a growth-rate approximation.
cards.source: Chapter 4 · Long-run money and prices · authored companion

cards.title: If E starts at 1, jumps to 1.30, then settles at 1.10 dollars per euro, what is the overshoot?
cards.answer: The initial 30% rise exceeds the eventual 10% rise. E later falls from 1.30 to 1.10: a partial dollar recovery, not a return to its original value.
cards.takeaway: Separate the immediate move, reversal, and lasting change.
cards.source: Chapter 4 · Overshooting and expectations · authored companion

cards.title: With domestic inflation 6% and foreign inflation 2%, what does relative PPP predict for domestic depreciation?
cards.answer: Approximately 4%. Exactly, \(E_{1}/E_{0}-1=\frac{1.06}{1.02}-1\approx 3.92\%\).
cards.takeaway: An inflation differential is the linear approximation to a gross-price ratio.
cards.source: Chapter 5 · Purchasing power parity · authored companion

cards.title: If E rises 10% and domestic P rises 10% while foreign P stays fixed, what happens to q?
cards.answer: It is unchanged: the 1.10 multiplier in E cancels the 1.10 multiplier in P. There is nominal depreciation but no real depreciation.
cards.takeaway: Currency units can move without changing relative goods prices.
cards.source: Chapter 5 · Real exchange rates · authored companion

cards.title: If expected inflation rises from 2% to 5% and the real rate stays at 1%, how does the approximate nominal rate change?
cards.answer: It rises from 3% to 6%, a three-percentage-point increase.
cards.takeaway: The Fisher effect compensates for expected purchasing-power loss.
cards.source: Chapter 5 · Fisher effect and inflation · authored companion

cards.title: If q rises 8% but \(P/P^{*}\) falls 10%, what happens to \(E=q\frac{P}{P^*}\)?
cards.answer: E changes by \(1.08\times 0.90-1=-2.8\%\), a nominal appreciation despite real depreciation. Different magnitudes could reverse the net sign.
cards.takeaway: Opposing channels must be combined quantitatively.
cards.source: Chapter 5 · Real demand and supply · authored companion

cards.title: If domestic and foreign nominal rates are 7% and 4%, and expected inflation is 4% and 2%, what expected real depreciation is implied?
cards.answer: Real rates are approximately 3% and 2%, so real parity implies 1% expected domestic real depreciation. The nominal gap is 3 points; the inflation gap accounts for 2.
cards.takeaway: Subtract inflation before interpreting a real-return gap.
cards.source: Chapter 5 · Real interest parity · authored companion

cards.title: If 1 and 3 are exact machine numbers, must their quotient be exact?
cards.answer: No. \(1/3\) has a repeating binary expansion, so it must be rounded. Exactly stored inputs do not guarantee an exactly representable result.
cards.takeaway: Input accuracy and arithmetic rounding are separate issues.

cards.title: Does rounding make swapping two finite operands change their sum?
cards.answer: With the same IEEE format and rounding mode, no: \(a+b\) and \(b+a\) round the same exact sum. Regrouping three terms can change intermediate rounding. Exclude NaNs and changes in evaluation precision.
cards.takeaway: Swapping two operands differs from regrouping a longer calculation.

cards.title: How far apart are binary64 numbers between \(2^{54}\) and \(2^{55}\)?
cards.answer: The gaps within this interval are \(2^{54-52}=4\). The gap immediately above \(2^{55}\) is 8. Binary64 has 53 significant binary bits.
cards.takeaway: One power-of-two interval has one spacing; the next doubles it.

cards.title: What does binary64 compute for \(2^{54}+1\) with nearest rounding?
cards.answer: \(2^{54}\). The neighboring machine numbers are \(2^{54}\) and \(2^{54}+4\); the exact result is closer to the first. This is not a halfway tie.
cards.takeaway: Compare the increment with the local gap.

cards.title: Why does multiplying two upper-triangular matrices keep zeros below the diagonal?
cards.answer: For \(i>j\), a nonzero term in \((AB)_{ij}=\sum_k A_{ik}B_{kj}\) would need both \(k\ge i\) and \(k\le j\). That is impossible.
cards.takeaway: Both triangular patterns rule out every contribution below the diagonal.

cards.title: Must a lower-triangular matrix times an upper-triangular matrix be triangular?
cards.answer: No. For example, \[\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}.\] The product has nonzero entries on both sides of the diagonal.
cards.takeaway: Opposite triangular patterns can fill each other’s zeros.

cards.title: When is the product of two real symmetric matrices also symmetric?
cards.answer: Exactly when they commute: \(AB=BA\). Since \((AB)^T=B^TA^T=BA\), symmetry of each factor alone is not enough.
cards.takeaway: Transposing a product reverses its order.

cards.title: Can a singular matrix still have an LU factorization?
cards.answer: Yes. \(\operatorname{diag}(1,0)=I\operatorname{diag}(1,0)\) is an LU factorization. Singularity means at least one zero diagonal entry in the triangular factor; it does not prohibit the factorization.
cards.takeaway: Having factors does not guarantee that triangular solves are invertible.

cards.title: For \(x=(1,1)\), which is largest: its 1-, 2-, or infinity-norm?
cards.answer: The 1-norm is 2, the 2-norm is \(\sqrt2\), and the infinity-norm is 1. Generally, \(\|x\|_\infty\le\|x\|_2\le\|x\|_1\).
cards.takeaway: Largest component, Euclidean length, and total absolute size measure different things.

cards.title: Does a singular matrix have zero matrix norm?
cards.answer: No. \(A=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)\) is singular but \(\|A\|_2=1\). Singularity means some direction is destroyed, while the 2-norm measures the largest stretch.
cards.takeaway: One collapsed direction does not erase every direction.

cards.title: Can a nonzero matrix have zero 1-, 2-, infinity-, or Frobenius norm?
cards.answer: No. Each is a norm, and a norm is zero only for the zero matrix. In particular, \(\|A\|_2=0\) means \(Ax=0\) for every unit vector, so every column is zero.
cards.takeaway: Zero size is stronger than a zero determinant.

cards.title: If \(Ax_1=Ax_2=b\), why is every point on their line another solution?
cards.answer: For any real \(t\), \[A((1-t)x_1+tx_2)=(1-t)b+tb=b.\] If \(x_1\ne x_2\), varying \(t\) gives infinitely many distinct solutions.
cards.takeaway: The coefficients add to one, keeping the same right-hand side.

cards.title: If you reorder the rows of both A and b, does the solution change?
cards.answer: No. \(PAx=Pb\) contains the same equations in a different order. Multiplying by \(P^T=P^{-1}\) restores \(Ax=b\). Reordering A without b generally changes the problem.
cards.takeaway: Move each equation together with its right-hand side.

cards.title: If \(Ax=b\), which vector solves \(APz=b\) for a permutation matrix P?
cards.answer: \(z=P^Tx\), because \(Pz=x\). Column permutations reorder the unknowns, so the entries must be relabeled when reporting the original solution.
cards.takeaway: Columns correspond to variables; rows correspond to equations.

cards.title: Why does an invertible left multiplier M preserve the solutions of \(Ax=b\)?
cards.answer: \(Ax=b\) implies \(MAx=Mb\). Conversely, multiply the transformed system by \(M^{-1}\). If M is singular, this reverse step fails and information can be lost.
cards.takeaway: Reversible equation transformations preserve exactly the same constraints.

cards.title: Multiply A and b by nonzero \(\alpha\). What changes for a fixed estimate \(\hat x\)?
cards.answer: The exact solution is unchanged, but the residual becomes \(r_{\mathrm{new}}=\alpha(b-A\hat x)=\alpha r\). Its norm scales by \(|\alpha|\), even though the estimate has not improved.
cards.takeaway: Raw residual size depends on the units used for the equations.

cards.title: Can scaling individual equations improve conditioning without changing their solution?
cards.answer: Yes. Let \(A=\operatorname{diag}(1,10^{-6})\) and \(D=\operatorname{diag}(1,10^6)\). Then \(DA=I\): its condition number drops from \(10^6\) to 1. Use \(Db\) too; the exact solution stays the same.
cards.takeaway: Relative equation scales affect numerical conditioning.

cards.title: If a first column is \((2,1)^T\), can row scaling change the partial pivot?
cards.answer: Yes. Initially the first row wins. Multiplying row 2 by 3 makes the column \((2,3)^T\), so the second row wins. Scale its right-hand side too to preserve the system.
cards.takeaway: Pivot choices depend on the magnitudes after scaling.

cards.title: What are the first pivots with no, partial, and complete pivoting?
cards.answer: No pivoting: 4. Partial pivoting: 6, the largest magnitude in column 1. Complete pivoting: −10, the largest magnitude anywhere in the active matrix.
cards.takeaway: The search region determines which entry becomes the pivot.

cards.title: For dense \(A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), why compute \(x(x^TA)\) instead of \((xx^T)A\)?
cards.answer: Compute the row \(x^TA\) in \(O(n^2)\), then its outer product with x in \(O(n^2)\). Forming \(xx^T\) and using ordinary dense matrix multiplication costs \(O(n^3)\). Both expressions give the same matrix in exact arithmetic.
cards.takeaway: Choose parentheses that preserve the cheap low-rank structure.

cards.title: How do you solve \(LPx=b\) when L is invertible lower triangular?
cards.answer: Solve \(Ly=b\) by forward substitution, then set \(x=P^Ty\). The intermediate variable is \(y=Px\).
cards.takeaway: Undo the permutation after the triangular solve.

cards.title: How do you solve \(PLx=b\) when L is invertible lower triangular?
cards.answer: First form \(P^Tb\), then solve \(Lx=P^Tb\) by forward substitution. Here the permutation acts on the output, so undo it on b.
cards.takeaway: The factor order tells you where to apply the inverse permutation.

cards.title: When can least squares make its residual exactly zero?
cards.answer: Exactly when b lies in the column space of A: some linear combination of A’s columns equals b. Then the minimum of \(\|Ax-b\|_2\) is zero.
cards.takeaway: An exact fit requires the target to be reachable.

cards.title: Does a zero least-squares residual guarantee unique coefficients?
cards.answer: No. With \(A=[1\;1]\) and \(b=1\), every pair satisfying \(x_1+x_2=1\) fits exactly. A nonzero null-space direction changes coefficients without changing the fitted value.
cards.takeaway: Perfect prediction does not imply identifiable coefficients.

cards.title: Does an arbitrary Householder reflection automatically zero the tail of any vector?
cards.answer: No. Its reflecting direction must be chosen from the vector being reduced. For example, \(H=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1)\) sends \((1,1)^T\) to \((-1,1)^T\), leaving the second entry nonzero.
cards.takeaway: A reflection has the desired zeros only when designed for that target.

cards.title: Why do least-squares coefficients satisfy \(A^TAx=A^Tb\)?
cards.answer: At the minimum, the residual \(b-Ax\) is perpendicular to every column of A. Thus \(A^T(b-Ax)=0\), giving the normal equations. They hold even when the minimizing coefficients are not unique.
cards.takeaway: The leftover error cannot have a component along a direction you can fit.

cards.title: Are normal equations strictly worse conditioned for every full-column-rank A?
cards.answer: No. \(\kappa_2(A^TA)=\kappa_2(A)^2\), but when \(\kappa_2(A)=1\), both equal 1. For example, A with orthonormal columns has \(A^TA=I\).
cards.takeaway: Squaring increases numbers greater than one, not one itself.

cards.title: How can you check whether two real vectors are perpendicular?
cards.answer: Compute their dot product: \(x^Ty=0\). For example, \((1,2)^T\) and \((2,-1)^T\) are perpendicular because \(2-2=0\).
cards.takeaway: Positive and negative contributions cancel exactly.

cards.title: If x is perpendicular to y and y to z, must x be perpendicular to z?
cards.answer: No. Take \(x=z=(1,0)^T\) and \(y=(0,1)^T\). Both are perpendicular to y, but \(x^Tz=1\).
cards.takeaway: Sharing a perpendicular direction does not make two vectors perpendicular.

cards.title: For a square orthogonal Q, what are its 2-norm, condition number, and Frobenius norm?
cards.answer: \(\|Q\|_2=1\), \(\kappa_2(Q)=1\), and \(\|Q\|_F=\sqrt n\) for \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\). Every singular value is 1; the Frobenius norm combines their squares.
cards.takeaway: No direction stretches, but the total squared size counts n directions.

cards.title: Is \(Q=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\) orthogonal?
cards.answer: Yes. Its columns are perpendicular unit vectors, so \(Q^TQ=I\). It rotates every vector by 90 degrees without changing its length.
cards.takeaway: Orthogonal columns give a length-preserving coordinate transformation.

cards.title: For nonzero w, what makes \(H=I-2ww^T\) orthogonal?
cards.answer: \(w^Tw=1\). Along w, H multiplies by \(1-2\|w\|_2^2\), which must be −1 for nonzero w. For an unnormalized vector v, use \(H=I-2vv^T/(v^Tv)\).
cards.takeaway: Normalize the reflecting direction, or divide by its squared length.

cards.title: Does \(H=I-2ww^T\) need unit-length w to be symmetric?
cards.answer: No. \((ww^T)^T=ww^T\), so \(H^T=H\) for any real w. Unit length is required for this formula to be an orthogonal reflection, not for symmetry.
cards.takeaway: Symmetry and length preservation are different properties.

cards.title: For unit w, which parts of a vector does \(I-2ww^T\) change?
cards.answer: Write \(x=aw+z\) with \(w^Tz=0\). Then \(Hx=-aw+z\): the component along w flips, while every perpendicular component stays fixed.
cards.takeaway: A reflection reverses one direction and preserves its perpendicular plane.

cards.title: If an orthogonal Q sends \((1,1)^T\) to \((\alpha,0)^T\), what can \(\alpha\) be?
cards.answer: \(\alpha=\pm\sqrt2\). Length preservation fixes \(|\alpha|\), not its sign. Householder QR concentrates a column’s remaining Euclidean length in one entry while zeroing the entries below it.
cards.takeaway: The squared length survives even when coordinates disappear.

cards.title: Why is \(\kappa_2(A)=\sigma_{\max}/\sigma_{\min}\) for invertible A?
cards.answer: The largest stretch of A is \(\sigma_{\max}\). The inverse has largest stretch \(1/\sigma_{\min}\), because it reverses A’s weakest direction. Multiply the two norms.
cards.takeaway: Sensitivity compares the strongest and weakest directions.

cards.title: How many Householder reflections suffice to triangularize a square \(n\times n\) matrix?
cards.answer: At most \(n-1\). Each step clears the entries below one diagonal position. The last column has no entries below its diagonal, so it needs no reflection. Some steps can be skipped if the entries are already zero.
cards.takeaway: Count tails that need clearing, not columns alone.

cards.title: With reduced SVD \(A=U_r\Sigma_rV_r^T\), how do you get the minimum-norm least-squares solution?
cards.answer: \(x=V_r\Sigma_r^{-1}U_r^Tb\). Project b onto the nonzero left singular directions, divide by their singular values, then combine the right singular directions. Set null-space coefficients to zero.
cards.takeaway: Fit reachable directions and avoid adding invisible coefficient components.

cards.title: If reduced Q has orthonormal columns spanning A’s column space, what does \(QQ^Tb\) do?
cards.answer: It projects b onto the possible fitted vectors. If b is in that space, \(QQ^Tb=b\); if b is perpendicular to it, \(QQ^Tb=0\). Use reduced Q: a full square orthogonal Q would give \(QQ^T=I\).
cards.takeaway: Keep only directions the model can express.

cards.title: Can you build a 2×2 matrix whose columns span \((1,1)^T\) but not \((1,-1)^T\)?
cards.answer: Use \(A=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}\). Every column combination has equal coordinates, so \((1,1)^T\) is reachable and \((1,-1)^T\) is not.
cards.takeaway: Choose columns along the direction you want to keep.

cards.title: Can a 2×2 matrix have 2-norm 4 and Frobenius norm 5?
cards.answer: Yes: \(A=\operatorname{diag}(4,3)\). Its largest singular value is 4, while \(\|A\|_F=\sqrt{4^2+3^2}=5\).
cards.takeaway: The spectral norm takes the maximum; the Frobenius norm combines all directions.

cards.title: Does a rectangular or singular real matrix still have an SVD?
cards.answer: Yes. Every real matrix has \(A=U\Sigma V^T\), with orthogonal factors and nonnegative singular values. Rectangular shape changes dimensions; singularity introduces zero singular values.
cards.takeaway: An SVD does not require an inverse.

cards.title: Must an orthogonal matrix have determinant +1?
cards.answer: No. Taking determinants of \(Q^TQ=I\) gives \((\det Q)^2=1\), so \(\det Q=\pm1\). A reflection such as \(\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\) has determinant −1.
cards.takeaway: Length preservation allows orientation reversal.

cards.title: Can swapping two finite floating-point factors change their rounded product?
cards.answer: Under the same IEEE format and rounding mode, no. Both orders round the same exact product. This does not mean regrouping several factors is harmless. Exclude NaNs and changes in evaluation precision.
cards.takeaway: A single rounded multiplication remains commutative.

cards.title: When is a real diagonal matrix orthogonal?
cards.answer: Exactly when every diagonal entry is +1 or −1. For \(D=\operatorname{diag}(d_i)\), \(D^TD=\operatorname{diag}(d_i^2)\), which equals I only if every \(d_i^2=1\).
cards.takeaway: Sign flips preserve length; arbitrary scaling does not.

cards.title: Given a nonzero pivot \(a_{ij}\), how do its column and row form a rank-one approximation?
cards.answer: \(B=A_{:j}A_{i:}/a_{ij}\). Dividing by the pivot makes B match both the chosen column and chosen row. Consequently, \(A-B\) is zero on that row and column.
cards.takeaway: One cross samples a column direction and its row weights.

cards.title: For this matrix, what rank-one approximation uses the complete pivot 9?
cards.answer: \[B=\frac19\begin{bmatrix}3\\6\\9\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}7&8&9\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}7/3&8/3&3\\14/3&16/3&6\\7&8&9\end{bmatrix}.\] It matches the final row and column exactly.
cards.takeaway: Divide by the shared entry to avoid counting its scale twice.

cards.title: A stable binary64 solve keeps about 6 of 16 digits. What condition-number scale might explain this?
cards.answer: Roughly \(10^{10}\): the rule of thumb is digits lost \(\approx\log_{10}\kappa(A)\). This is a worst-case sensitivity estimate, not proof of the exact condition number from one observed error.
cards.takeaway: Ten lost digits suggest ten orders of possible amplification.

cards.title: How much storage does \(A=BC\) need for a 10000×10000 rank-100 matrix?
cards.answer: B is 10000×100 and C is 100×10000, so together they store 2,000,000 numbers. A dense A stores 100,000,000: 50 times as many.
cards.takeaway: Store the smaller factors when a few directions explain the whole map.

cards.title: How many multiplications compute \(Ax\) using 10000×100 B and 100×10000 C?
cards.answer: Compute \(y=Cx\), then \(By\). Each stage takes 1,000,000 multiplications, totaling 2,000,000, versus 100,000,000 for dense A. Do not form BC first.
cards.takeaway: Keep the intermediate vector in the small 100-dimensional space.

cards.title: What does a rank-100 map in \(\mathbb R^{10000}\) do to the unit ball?
cards.answer: It produces a bounded ellipsoid lying in a 100-dimensional column space. Its nonzero singular values are the semiaxis lengths. The image is not the entire subspace: input lengths are bounded.
cards.takeaway: Rank counts surviving directions, while the unit-ball constraint bounds their extent.

cards.title: For full-column-rank A, when do two targets give the same least-squares coefficients?
cards.answer: When \(A^T(b_1-b_2)=0\): their difference is perpendicular to A’s column space. Equivalently, their projections onto the possible fitted vectors are equal.
cards.takeaway: Changing only the unfit part of the data leaves coefficients unchanged.

cards.title: For unit w, why does \((I-2ww^T)^T(I-2ww^T)=I\)?
cards.answer: Expand: \[I-4ww^T+4w(w^Tw)w^T.\] Since \(w^Tw=1\), the last two terms cancel. Thus H preserves length; symmetry also gives \(H^2=I\).
cards.takeaway: Reflecting twice restores the original vector.

cards.title: To convert orthogonal columns into SVD columns, what must you do first?
cards.answer: Normalize them and absorb their lengths into the middle scaling. For \(C=[(1,0,1)^T\;(0,1,0)^T]\), the column lengths are \(\sqrt2\) and 1. Orthogonal is not the same as orthonormal.
cards.takeaway: Singular vectors have unit length; singular values carry the stretching.

cards.title: What are the singular values of \(A=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\-1&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}\)?
cards.answer: \(A^TA=\begin{bmatrix}3&1\\1&3\end{bmatrix}\), with eigenvalues 4 and 2. The singular values are their square roots: 2 and \(\sqrt2\).
cards.takeaway: The squared stretches appear as eigenvalues of the Gram matrix.

cards.title: For the displayed A, if \(v_1=(1,1)^T/\sqrt2\), what is its matching left singular vector?
cards.answer: \(Av_1=(\sqrt2,0,\sqrt2)^T\). Its length is 2, so \(u_1=Av_1/2=(1,0,1)^T/\sqrt2\). Similarly, \(v_2=(-1,1)^T/\sqrt2\) gives \(u_2=(0,1,0)^T\) and \(\sigma_2=\sqrt2\).
cards.takeaway: Apply A to a unit input direction, then normalize the output.

cards.title: Can a negative middle factor be left as a negative singular value?
cards.answer: No. Singular values are nonnegative. Absorb a negative sign into a singular vector instead. Once an SVD is formed, flipping both \(u_i\) and \(v_i\) leaves \(\sigma_i u_iv_i^T\) unchanged.
cards.takeaway: Sign choices belong to directions, not stretch magnitudes.

cards.title: Why can the closest fit in infinity-norm differ from the perpendicular Euclidean fit?
cards.answer: An infinity-norm ball is an axis-aligned square in 2D, while a Euclidean ball is a circle. Expand the appropriate shape around b until it touches the line of possible fits. The first contact can occur at different points.
cards.takeaway: Changing the error measure changes which discrepancy matters most.

cards.title: Fit \(b=(1,0)^T\) by \((t,2t)^T\). Which t minimizes the largest absolute coordinate error?
cards.answer: \(t=1/3\). Balance \(1-t=2t\), giving maximum error \(2/3\). The residual has equal-magnitude coordinates. This corner-contact geometry explains the 45-degree direction in the quiz figure; it is not universal for every line.
cards.takeaway: The best worst-coordinate fit balances the competing errors.

cards.title: For the same fit \((t,2t)^T\) to \((1,0)^T\), what does ordinary least squares choose?
cards.answer: \(t=1/5\), because minimizing \((t-1)^2+4t^2\) gives \(10t-2=0\). This differs from the infinity-norm optimum \(1/3\).
cards.takeaway: Least squares balances squared errors; infinity-norm controls the worst coordinate.

cards.title: What matrix properties help accurate linear solves versus low-rank compression?
cards.answer: Solves benefit from a modest condition number and a stable algorithm. Compression benefits from rapidly decaying singular values, so discarded directions contribute little. A large condition number alone does not guarantee a useful low-rank approximation.
cards.takeaway: Invertibility needs every direction; compression deliberately discards weak ones.

cards.title: Does \(A=\operatorname{diag}(1,\ldots,1,10^{-12})\) have a good rank-one approximation?
cards.answer: Not when there are many unit entries. Its condition number is huge, but dropping to rank one discards many equally strong directions. Only the final direction is tiny.
cards.takeaway: A ratio of extremes does not describe the whole singular-value spectrum.

cards.title: What is the rank of this cross-shaped matrix?
cards.answer: 2. Columns 1 and 3 are identical, giving an upper bound of 2. Columns 1 and 2 are independent, so the rank is at least 2.
cards.takeaway: Prove rank with both a construction and an independence check.

cards.title: How can two outer products build the displayed cross-shaped matrix?
cards.answer: \[A=\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\\0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1&1&1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\\1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0&1&0\end{bmatrix}.\] The first builds the middle row; the second adds the top and bottom of the middle column.
cards.takeaway: Avoid double-counting the central pixel.

cards.title: For dense LU, how does factoring a 2n×n matrix compare with an n×n matrix?
cards.answer: The leading cost for \(m\ge n\) is \(mn^2-n^3/3\). The ratio is \((2-1/3)/(1-1/3)=5/2\). Doubling rows while fixing columns is different from doubling both dimensions.
cards.takeaway: Elimination work shrinks across successive columns.

cards.title: Does dense Householder QR have the same 2n×n versus n×n cost ratio as LU?
cards.answer: Yes, to leading order. QR costs \(2mn^2-2n^3/3\), twice the corresponding LU formula. That common factor cancels in the ratio, again giving \(5/2\).
cards.takeaway: Cost ratios depend on shape as well as the factorization.

cards.title: Why can \(\|AB\|_2\) never exceed \(\|A\|_2\|B\|_2\)?
cards.answer: For every unit x, \(\|ABx\|_2\le\|A\|_2\|Bx\|_2\le\|A\|_2\|B\|_2\). Maximize over x. Each stage can stretch by at most its own maximum.
cards.takeaway: The maximum combined stretch cannot beat the product of individual maxima.

cards.title: For nonzero A and B, when does \(\|AB\|_2=\|A\|_2\|B\|_2\)?
cards.answer: When some input maximally stretched by B is sent into an input direction maximally stretched by A. Equivalently, B’s top left-singular subspace intersects A’s top right-singular subspace nontrivially. With repeated top singular values, one compatible direction is enough.
cards.takeaway: The strongest directions must connect across the two maps.

cards.title: For \(A=\operatorname{diag}(2,1)\), which B attains the product-of-norms bound?
cards.answer: \(B=\operatorname{diag}(3,1)\) gives \(AB=\operatorname{diag}(6,1)\), attaining \(2\cdot3=6\). With \(B=\operatorname{diag}(1,3)\), the product is \(\operatorname{diag}(2,3)\), whose norm is only 3.
cards.takeaway: Strong stretches reinforce each other only when their directions line up.

cards.title: Can a computed \(A^TA\) be symmetric even when its entries have rounding error?
cards.answer: Yes. Paired entries use the same products in reverse operand order. If both dot products use identical summation order, precision, and rounding, their results agree. Different reduction orders can break exact symmetry; do not assume it for every implementation.
cards.takeaway: Rounding error and loss of symmetry are separate questions.

cards.title: In the first symmetric Householder step on a 5×5 matrix, which entries are deliberately zeroed?
cards.answer: Entries \((3,1),(4,1),(5,1)\) and their symmetric partners \((1,3),(1,4),(1,5)\). The first subdiagonal entry is retained. Two-sided updates preserve symmetry while moving toward tridiagonal form.
cards.takeaway: Symmetric reduction clears beyond the first off-diagonal, not every off-diagonal entry.

cards.title: With \(H=\operatorname{diag}(1,\widetilde H)\), which entry of \(H^TAH\) is guaranteed to equal A’s?
cards.answer: The top-left entry: \(e_1^TH^TAHe_1=e_1^TAe_1=A_{11}\), because \(He_1=e_1\). Other entries may coincide for special A, but are not generally fixed.
cards.takeaway: Leaving the first basis vector unchanged protects its quadratic-form value.

cards.title: Why use \(H^TAH\) rather than only \(HA\) in symmetric eigenvalue reduction?
cards.answer: For orthogonal H, \(H^T=H^{-1}\), so the two-sided update is a similarity transformation. It preserves eigenvalues and, for symmetric A, symmetry. A one-sided QR update need not preserve A’s eigenvalues.
cards.takeaway: Change coordinates on both sides to represent the same linear map.

cards.title: Does forming \(A+A^T\) guarantee that Cholesky can be used?
cards.answer: No. It guarantees symmetry, not positive definiteness. For \(A=-I\), the sum is \(-2I\), which is negative definite. Standard real Cholesky needs a symmetric positive-definite matrix.
cards.takeaway: Check the sign of quadratic forms before choosing Cholesky.

cards.title: When Cholesky applies, how does its dense factorization cost compare with LU?
cards.answer: Cholesky takes about \(n^3/3\) floating-point operations, versus \(2n^3/3\) for general LU. Its symmetry lets it do roughly half the leading work.
cards.takeaway: Structure saves work only when the required assumptions hold.

cards.title: Using pivot 2, what rank-one approximation does this matrix produce?
cards.answer: \[B=\begin{bmatrix}1/2&1/2&1/2&1\\1/2&1/2&1/2&1\\1&1&1&2\end{bmatrix}.\] It is column 4 times row 3, divided by the pivot 2.
cards.takeaway: The chosen row and column are matched exactly.

cards.title: A rank-one residual has six entries equal to 1/2 and every other entry zero. What is its Frobenius norm?
cards.answer: \(\sqrt{6(1/2)^2}=\sqrt{3/2}\). Square each entry, sum them, then take the square root. This is the error of the quiz’s one-step complete-pivot approximation.
cards.takeaway: Frobenius error combines entrywise errors in quadrature.

cards.title: For fixed full-column-rank A, can a target perturbation of length \(\varepsilon\) move its least-squares fit farther than \(\varepsilon\)?
cards.answer: No. The fitted-vector change is \(\delta\hat b=P\delta b\), with \(P=QQ^T\). Orthogonal projection cannot increase Euclidean length, so \(\|\delta\hat b\|_2\le\varepsilon\).
cards.takeaway: Discarding the perpendicular component cannot enlarge a vector.

cards.title: Can least-squares coefficients change greatly even when the fitted vector barely changes?
cards.answer: Yes. \(\delta x=A^+\delta b\), so \(\|\delta x\|_2\le\|\delta b\|_2/\sigma_{\min}(A)\). A tiny smallest singular value allows large coefficient changes, while the fitted-vector change remains bounded by \(\|\delta b\|_2\).
cards.takeaway: Large, canceling coefficient changes can have small prediction effects.

cards.title: Which target perturbation maximizes coefficient change in full-column-rank least squares?
cards.answer: \(\delta b=\varepsilon u_{\min}\), along the weakest left singular direction. Then \(\delta x=(\varepsilon/\sigma_{\min})v_{\min}\). A perturbation perpendicular to the column space instead changes no coefficient.
cards.takeaway: Noise matters most when it points along the model’s weakest identifiable direction.

cards.title: For invertible square A and B, why is \(\kappa_2(AB)\le\kappa_2(A)\kappa_2(B)\)?
cards.takeaway: Both the forward map and its inverse contribute to sensitivity.

cards.title: If \(\|A\|_2=\|B\|_2=1\) and both condition numbers are 2, how large can \(\kappa_2(AB)\) be?
cards.answer: At most 4, and 4 is attainable. Take \(A=B=\operatorname{diag}(1,1/2)\); then \(AB=\operatorname{diag}(1,1/4)\), whose condition number is 4.
cards.takeaway: Aligned weak directions compound the loss of relative scale.

cards.title: If A and B each have norm 1 and condition number 2, must A+B be well-conditioned?
cards.answer: No. Choose \(A=\operatorname{diag}(1,1/2)\) and \(B=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1/2)\). Each has condition number 2, but \(A+B=\operatorname{diag}(2,0)\) is singular. There is no analogous finite bound for the sum.
cards.takeaway: Adding two reliable maps can cancel an entire direction.
